parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *židъkъ (“liquid, watery”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žila.

parole.significato: residential (relating to a place of personal residence)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žilъ. By surface analysis, жить (žitʹ) + -лой (-loj).

parole.significato: fat or oil from the body of an animal
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic жиръ (žirŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žirъ.

parole.significato: grain (any unground grain, such as rye, wheat, buckwheat, millet, barley, maize, oats)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žito (“grain, corn”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *géiˀtan, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃tom, from *gʷeyh₃-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žiti (compare Belarusian жыць (žycʹ), Ukrainian жи́ти (žýty), Old Church Slavonic жити (žiti)), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeih₃w- (“to live”). Cognate to Lithuanian gyventi, Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati, “lives”), Latin vīvō, and English quick.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žitьje, from Proto-Slavic *žiti (“to live”). Doublet of житие́ (žitijé), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: to squint, to narrow one's eyes
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьžuriti via metathesis. Cognate to Russian мига́ть (migátʹ), Russian миг (mig), Russian мгнове́ние (mgnovénije). Possibly influenced by жму (žmu).

parole.significato: ass, arse (the buttocks of a person or animal)
parole.testo: Uncertain, presumed to derive from a Proto-Slavic form which cannot be easily reconstructed. According to Vasmer, two probable hypotheses are: * Cognate with Polish gap (“rubbernecker”) and gapić się (“to stare”) * Cognate with Old Church Slavonic жупа (župa, “hole”) and Ukrainian жу́па (žúpa, “salt
Inherited from Old East Slavic жьрати (žĭrati), from Proto-Slavic *žьrati, related to English devour and voracity. Compare Ukrainian же́рти (žérty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьrьcь, from *žьrti + *-ьcь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *girˀ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic жужелица (žuželica), from Proto-Slavic *žuželica.

parole.significato: to hum, to buzz, to drone, to whirr
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žužati. Onomatopoeic.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žukъ. Per Vasmer (and others) likely related to жужжа́ть (žužžátʹ), жу́желица (žúželica). Per Chernykh, however, likely related to Proto-Slavic *govędo (denied by Anikin).

Inherited from Old East Slavic жеравль (žeravlĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žeravľь. Cognates include Belarusian жураве́ль (žuravjélʹ) and Ukrainian жураве́ль (žuravélʹ). Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žuriti. Cognate with Ukrainian жури́ти (žurýty, “to sadden”), Belarusian жури́цца (žurícca, “to grieve”), Serbo-Croatian жу́рити (“to hurry (intransitive)”), Slovene žúriti (“to force, to rush, to hurry (transitive)”) (tonal orthography). Per Vasmer, related to Serbo-Cro

Inherited from Old East Slavic жолобъ (žolobŭ), from Proto-Slavic *želbъ, , from Proto-Indo-European *gelbh-, *gelebh-. Cognate with Church Slavic жлѣбъ (žlěbŭ), Ukrainian жо́лоб (žólob), Belarusian жо́лаб (žólab), Bulgarian жлеб (žleb), Serbo-Croatian жлије̑б, ждлије̑б, жле̑б, Slovene žlȇb, Old Cze
From Old East Slavic жьлтъ (žĭltŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žьltъ (“yellow”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gilˀtás, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”), whence English yellow.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želǫdь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gel-, *gil-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьlčь.
From Old East Slavic женъка (ženŭka), from Proto-Slavic *ženъka.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьrny, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gírˀnūˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥h₂-n-uH-. Cognates include Sanskrit ग्रावन् (grāvan), Old Armenian երկան (erkan) and Old English cweorn (English quern).

Inherited from Old East Slavic жестъкъ (žestŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žestъkъ. Cognate to Old Church Slavonic жестъ (žestŭ, “hard”), жестѣти (žestěti, “to harden”). Also related to жесто́кий (žestókij, “cruel”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *za.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zabavьnъ. Compare typologically заня́тный (zanjátnyj), захва́тывающий (zaxvátyvajuščij).
Inherited from Old East Slavic забороло (zaborolo), from Proto-Slavic *zabordlo. Doublet of забра́ло (zabrálo), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic.

From Old East Slavic зобота (zobota), from Proto-Slavic [Term?], possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gab- (“to watch, show”). Cognate with Proto-West Germanic *kapēn (“to watch, to look”), Proto-Germanic *kōpijaną (“to look after, care for”) (whence English keep). Also compare Ukrainian забо́та (zabó
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zabỳti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + быть (bytʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zavětъ, from *větъ (“talk, agreement”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zavistь. Cognate to Latin invidia (“envy”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic завътра (zavŭtra), from Proto-Slavic *za utra. By surface analysis, за (za) + у́тро (útro).
From Proto-Slavic *zajutrъkъ or Proto-Slavic *zautrъkъ, the same origin as Russian завтра (zavtra).

parole.significato: meat-fare day, cheese-fare day (the day before a fast, and thus the last day when food of animal origin may be eaten; t…
parole.testo: From загове́ть (zagovétʹ) + -енье (-enʹje), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *gověti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zadъ.

parole.significato: to dirty or wear out (usually clothes)
parole.testo: за- (za-) + дри́пать (drípatʹ), with дри́пать (drípatʹ) ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *dripa (“rag, tatter, cloth”).
East Slavic word inherited from Proto-Slavic *zakolti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + коло́ть (kolótʹ). Doublet of закла́ть (zaklátʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zakonъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫtъ. Compare Polish zakątek.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zalogъ.
From Proto-Slavic *zaměna.

parole.significato: lock (fastener that opens with a key, or part of a firearm)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zamъkъ, deverbal from *zamъknǫti (whence Russian замкну́ть (zamknútʹ)). Doublet of за́мок (zámok), a borrowing from Polish.
By surface analysis, за- (za-) + нозить (nozitʹ), further, from Proto-Slavic *nьziti. Cognate with вонзи́ть (vonzítʹ), пронзи́ть (pronzítʹ) and нож (nož).
Inherited from Old East Slavic западъ (zapadŭ, “sunset”), from Proto-Slavic *zapadъ, from *pasti. Compare Latin occidens.
Inherited from Old East Slavic заповѣдь (zapovědĭ), from Proto-Slavic *zapovědь.

parole.significato: binge, bout, drinking bout (recurring drunkenness due to a pathological craving for alcoholic drink; a period of contin…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zapojь. Compare запи́ть (zapítʹ). See *piti for more information.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaporъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaraza.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaraziti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + рази́ть (razítʹ, “to strike”).

parole.significato: negative oath or vow (solemn promise not to do something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zarokъ. Deverbal from early Proto-Slavic *zarekti (later *zareťi), with Indo-European ablaut typical of nouns. Compare заре́чь (zaréčʹ, “to prohibit, to force to renounce”), заре́чься (zaréčʹsja, “to renounce, to forswear”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zořa.

parole.significato: to sit down (to), to settle down (to), to set (to), to bury oneself (in)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zasěsti; compare Serbo-Croatian zàsjesti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + сесть (sestʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *zaslonъ, from *za- + *slonъ (“offset, cornice”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zasluga.

parole.significato: bolt, bar, latch (for locking a door, window, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatvorъ, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *verti. By surface analysis, deverbal from затворя́ть, затвори́ть (zatvorjátʹ, zatvorítʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tějati. Cognate with Belarusian заце́яць (zacjéjacʹ, “to undertake”) and (with a different prefix) Ukrainian ви́тіяти (výtijaty, “to undertake”). Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatopnъ. By surface analysis, deverbal from затону́ть (zatonútʹ)

parole.significato: congestion, obstruction, blockage, jam, traffic jam
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatorъ.

parole.significato: musty, smelling of dampness and rot
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatъxlъ. Per Vasmer, a variant of за́дхлый (zádxlyj). By surface analysis, за- (za-) + дох(ну́ть) (dox(nútʹ), “to breathe”) + -лый (-lyj). Also related to ту́хлый (túxlyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaučiti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + учи́ть (učítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaxodъ. By surface analysis, deverbal from заходи́ть (zaxodítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *začęti, also see Old Church Slavonic зачѧти (začęti).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zajęcь, *zajьcь. Compare typologically Finnish jänis (“hare; stowaway”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic зъвати (zŭvati), from Proto-Slavic *zъvati.

parole.significato: to ring, to jingle, to clink

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvěrinъ. By surface analysis, зверь (zverʹ) + -и́ный (-ínyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic звѣрь (zvěrĭ), from Proto-Slavic *zvěrь. Cognate with Ancient Greek θήρ (thḗr) and Latin ferus.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvonъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic звонити (zvoniti), from Proto-Slavic *zvoniti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvǫkъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ. Doublet of здра́вый (zdrávyj), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvьje. By surface analysis, здоро́вый (zdoróvyj) + -ье (-ʹje). Doublet of здра́вие (zdrávije), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dzělo. It could also be a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: potion (a small portion or dose of a liquid which is medicinal, poisonous, or magical)

From Proto-Slavic *zelenъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-; whence English yellow, gold, glow and chlorine.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zěnica.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьrno, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
Inherited from Old East Slavic зима (zima), from Proto-Slavic *zima, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źeimā́ˀ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰéyōm.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zimьnъ. By surface analysis, зима́ (zimá) + -ний (-nij).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zijati. Cognate with Lithuanian žióti (“to open (the mouth) wide”) (first singular žióju) žióvauti (“to yawn”), Latvian žàvât (“to yawn”), Ancient Greek χαίνω (khaínō, “to yawn”), χάσκω (kháskō, “to yawn”), Latin hiāre (“to yawn”), Sanskrit विहायस् (vihāyas, “airspace”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic зъло (zŭlo), from Proto-Slavic *zъlo.

parole.significato: bitterness (with regards to an animate being)

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlodějь. By surface analysis, зло (zlo) + -о- (-o-) + -дей (-dej), combining form of де́ять (déjatʹ, “to do”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źulas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwel-.

parole.significato: to slander, to traduce, to backbite (to make defamatory statements about another)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlosloviti. By surface analysis, зло (zlo, “evil”) + -о- (-o-) + сло́во (slóvo, “word”) + -ить (-itʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zmьjь. Doublet of змий (zmij), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. For the “kite” sense, compare New Latin draco volans (literally “flying dragon”), German Drachen (literally “dragon”), French cerf-volant < Old French serpe volant (literally “flying serpent”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zmьja. See also змей (zmej).
Inherited from Old East Slavic знакъ (znakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *znakъ, from *znati + *-kъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znamenьje.

parole.significato: famous, renowned, celebrated, noted, notorious, distinguished, eminent, illustrious
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *znamenitъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znamę.

parole.significato: to know: to be familiar with or accustomed to a person, place, or thing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic знати (znati), from Proto-Slavic *znati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źnōˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéh₃t (“to know, get to know”), from *ǵneh₃-. Cognates include Polish znać, English know, kenning, canny, German kennen and Sanskrit ज्ञा (jñā, “to know”). For the col
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znaxařь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *značiti. By surface analysis, знак (znak) + -ить (-itʹ).

parole.significato: to hit with a fever, chills, or shivers
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znobiti.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znojь. Cognate with Slovak znoj (“heat, sweat”), Polish znój (“heat”). An ancient stem in the form of -ju- is assumed. Compare dialectal Russian знеть (znetʹ), зне́ять (znéjatʹ, “to rot, to moulder, to incandesce”).
From Old East Slavic зобь (zobĭ), from Proto-Slavic *zobь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵebʰ- (“jaw, mouth”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zovъ. Compare звать (zvatʹ). See *zъvati for more information.
Inherited from Old East Slavic зьдъчии (zĭdŭčii, “potter, builder, bricklayer, mason”), from зьдъ (zĭdŭ, “stone wall”), зьдати (zĭdati), from Proto-Slavic *zьdati (“to build”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zola.

Cognates include Old Church Slavonic зълъва (zŭlŭva), Serbo-Croatian zaova, Polish zełwa, zołwa. Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъly, genitive *zъlъve, which is cognate to Latin glōs. See there for details.

Inherited from Old East Slavic желоза (želoza), from Proto-Slavic *želza, with distant assimilation ж…з > з…з. Cognate with Ukrainian за́лоза (záloza), Belarusian зало́за (zalóza). Compare железа́ (železá), from Old East Slavic железа (železa), with different treatment of the liquid diphthong.

Inherited from Old East Slavic золото (zoloto), from Proto-Slavic *zolto, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰolh₃tom (o-grade), from *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Doublet of зла́то (zláto), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злато (zlato). Compare Ukrainian золото (zoloto), Belarusian золата (zólata), Bulgari

Inherited from Old East Slavic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źámbas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos. Cognate to Old Church Slavonic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zǫbrъ. The politics sense compares supporters of a return to the old order with obsolete forms of life, i.e. the endangered bison.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zęba (whence also Polish zięba, Serbo-Croatian зеба). Compare typologically Macedonian снегар (snegar) (< снег (sneg) < Proto-Slavic *sněgъ). parole.significato: to be cold, to freeze, to feel cold
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zębnǫti.

parole.significato: land ploughed in autumn (for spring sowing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zębiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zętь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьgo, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm, from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic игра (igra), from Proto-Slavic *jьgra.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati. Cognate to Serbo-Croatian ȉgrati and Czech hrát.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ити (iti), from Proto-Slavic *jьti (“to go”). The infinitive spelled with д (d) is attested since the 14th century, under influence of иду́ (idú), идёшь (idjóšʹ), etc. Past tense шёл (šol) from Proto-Slavic *šьdlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьz, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵʰs, *h₁eǵʰs.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьz-; see *jьz for further information.

Inherited from Old East Slavic изъба, истъба (izŭba, istŭba), from Proto-Slavic *jьstъba, which may be related to Proto-West Germanic *stubu (“room, sitting room, oven”) (whence ultimately English stove) or to French étuve (“heated room, bathroom”), itself from Latin *extupāre. Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzvětъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzgъnanьje. By surface analysis, изгна́ть (izgnátʹ) + -а́ние (-ánije).

Inherited from Old East Slavic изгои (izgoi). Asynchronically analyzable as из- (iz-) + го́ить (góitʹ), from Proto-Slavic *gojiti (“to heal, feed”), the latter being a causative form of жить (žitʹ), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzgaga.
Related to Old Church Slavonic лихъ (lixŭ, “superfluous, excessive, bad”) from Proto-Slavic *lixъ (“remaining, unnecessary, superfluous, bad”).
From Old East Slavic измѣна (izměna), from Proto-Slavic *jьzměna.

parole.significato: to change, to alter, to modify, to edit
parole.testo: из- (iz-) + Old East Slavic мѣнити (měniti), from Proto-Slavic *měniti.

parole.significato: to depict, to picture, to portray
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzobraziti. Derived from о́браз (óbraz, “shape, image, figure”).

parole.significato: to utter, to speak solemnly / pompously
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzreťi. By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + -речь (-rečʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzučiti. By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + учи́ть (učítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьkati. By surface analysis, и (i, onomatopoeic) + -кать (-katʹ).

parole.significato: roe, spawn (of fish), also small eggs of frogs or other amphibia
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic икра (ikra), from Proto-Slavic *jьkrā, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ikrā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *yékʷr̥. Compare the semantic development of English roe; however, this is not an etymological cognate.
Inherited from Old East Slavic илъ (ilŭ), from Proto-Slavic *jьlъ. Compare Czech jíl, Polish ił.

parole.significato: elm, wych elm (Ulmus glabra) (tree or wood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьlьmъ.

parole.significato: to take, to grasp, to catch, to get, to acquire
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьmati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic именовати (imenovati), from Proto-Slavic *jьmenovati. By surface analysis, имен- (imen-, “name”) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьměti. Compare Belarusian мець (mjecʹ), Bulgarian имам (imam), Ukrainian ма́ти (máty), Polish mieć, Serbo-Croatian имати/imati, Old Church Slavonic имѣти (iměti).

parole.significato: personal name, first name, Christian name, given name (for inanimate things, see назва́ние (nazvánije))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic имѧ (imę), from Proto-Slavic *jьmę, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *inˀmin, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥. Cognates include English name and noun, Old Prussian emmens, Sanskrit नामन् (nāman), Persian نام (nâm), Ancient Greek ὄνομα (ónoma), Latin nōmen. Neologism sense: ca
By surface analysis, и́ней (ínej, “hoarfrost”) + -еть (-etʹ), with epenthetic д. Compare archaic/dialectal иневеть (inevetʹ). Possibly from Proto-Slavic *inьjevěti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьnьjь / *jьnьje / *jьnьja (“hoar-frost, rime”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic иногда (inogda), from Proto-Slavic *jьnogъda. By surface analysis, ино́й (inój) + -о- (-o-) + -гда (-gda); see когда́ (kogdá) for the origin of the last element.
Inherited from Old East Slavic инъ (inŭ) from Proto-Slavic *jь̀nъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *iˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁inos.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьskati. Cognate with Bulgarian и́скам (ískam, “I want”), Sanskrit इच्छति (icchati, “to desire”), Serbo-Croatian ѝскати, ìskati (“to look for”), Lithuanian ieškoti (“to seek”), Old English āscian (whence English ask).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьskra.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzkrьňь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьskriti. By surface analysis, и́скра (ískra) + -ить (-itʹ) + -ся (-sja) (stem-stressed variant) or и́скра (ískra) + -и́ть (-ítʹ) + -ся (-sja) (ending-stressed variant).
Inherited from Old East Slavic истꙑи (istyi), from Proto-Slavic *jistъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jixъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъ(n).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koblǫkъ.

parole.significato: censer, thurible (religious ornamental container for burning incense)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic кадило (kadilo, “incense”), from Proto-Slavic *kadidlo. By surface analysis, кади́ть (kadítʹ) + -ло (-lo).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kadidlьnica.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кадити (kaditi), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kadìti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кажьдꙑи (kažĭdyi), from Post Proto-Slavic *kažьdъ, from Proto-Slavic *kъžьdo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kāzàti.

parole.significato: to spoil, to ruin, to deform, to mar
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kazìti.

parole.significato: to execute, to put to death
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kazniti. Related to казнь (kaznʹ) and to каза́ть (kazátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kaznь.

parole.significato: how (in what way, in what manner) (translated as "what" with some verbs)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic како (kako), from Proto-Slavic *kako.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kaka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kakati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kakka-. Compare Serbo-Croatian kakati, kakiti, Italian cacare.
Inherited from Old East Slavic какъ (kakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kakъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kōkos.
Inherited from Old East Slavic калъ (kalŭ, “mud, muddy puddle, scum, sewage”), from Proto-Slavic *kalъ (“mud, swamp”).

parole.significato: kalach (traditional East Slavic bread shaped like a padlock or a wheel)
parole.testo: From кола́ч (koláč) (through akanye), from Proto-Slavic *kolačь, a derivation of *kolo (“circle, wheel”). By surface analysis, колесо́ (kolesó) + -ач (-ač). Cognate to Ukrainian кола́ч (koláč), Bulgarian кола́ч (koláč), Serbo-Croatian kòlač, Slovak koláč, Czech koláč, Polish kołacz.

parole.significato: guelder rose, snowball tree, Viburnum opulus
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kalina, further from Proto-Slavic *kalъ (whence Bulgarian кал (kal), Czech kal, Russian кал (kal)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kaliti (“to temper, case-harden”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic камень (kamenĭ), accusative of камꙑ (kamy), from Proto-Slavic *kamy.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kapnǫti. Doublet of ка́пнуть (kápnutʹ).

parole.significato: buzzard (any bird from the genus Buteo, or, sensu lato, from the subfamily Buteoninae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kanjukъ / *kanjakъ, from *kaňa, from Proto-Indo-European *kōnyā or *kan- (“to sing”), whence also Proto-Germanic *hanô (“rooster, cock”), Proto-Germanic *hanjō (“hen”) (whence English hen), Latin cicōnia (“stork”), Latin canō (“to sing”), Welsh canu, Ancient Greek καναχέ

parole.significato: to drip, to drop, to spill
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kapati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic каплꙗ (kaplja), from Proto-Slavic *kapľa, from *kapati + *-ja.

parole.significato: to drip, to drop, to spill
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kapnǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kara (“punishment”), from Proto-Indo-European *kor-. Cognate with Old Irish caire (“blame, disapproval”).

parole.significato: korovai (large, single-piece round or rectangular loaf of bread, elaborately decorated and served at a wedding)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic короваи (korovai), from Proto-Slavic *korvajь. Cognate with Ukrainian корова́й (korováj), Bulgarian крава́й (kraváj), Serbo-Croatian кра̀ва̄ј (“type of cake fed to the bride and groom”) (genitive крава́ја), Slovene kravȃj, krávaj. Per Vasmer, probably related to коро́в
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *karasь.

parole.significato: to punish, to chastise, to inflict penalty
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *karati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic касатисѧ (kasatisę), from Proto-Slavic *kasati + reflexive *sę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *katъ.

parole.significato: to drive (a trolley), to take (someone) for a drive
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ката́ти (katáti), from Proto-Slavic *katati.

parole.significato: to roll, to push (some object with wheels)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic катити (katiti), from Proto-Slavic *kotiti.

parole.significato: to rock, to swing, to shake, to wobble; to dandle
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kačati, iterative-durative for *kotiti (“to roll”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic каша (kaša), from Proto-Slavic *kaša. Cognates include Slovak kaša and Serbo-Croatian kaša.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kaš(ь)ľь (“cough”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kaʔs(u)lio-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s- (whence also English whoost).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kašьľati (“to cough”), from *kaš(ь)ľь (“cough”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kāˀsulia, *kāˀslia, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s- (whence also English whoost).

parole.significato: to repent (to feel sorrow or regret for what one has done or omitted to do)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic каꙗтисѧ (kajatisę), from Proto-Slavic *kàjati + reflexive -ся (-sja). Compare Ukrainian ка́ятися (kájatysja), Belarusian ка́яцца (kájacca).

parole.significato: kvass (a type of fermented no- or low-alcohol beverage, made from bread, often flavored with fruit)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic квасъ (kvasŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kvasъ (“leaven, fermented drink”). Cognate with Latin cāseus whence English cheese, and Sanskrit क्वथ् (kvath, “to boil”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kvasiti. By surface analysis, квас (kvas) + -ить (-itʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyvati.

parole.significato: to throw, to cast, to fling
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kydati. Cognate with English shoot.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyjь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyla.

parole.significato: to throw, to cast, to fling
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kydnǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English cupidity, covet and hope.

parole.significato: to boil (causative of кипе́ть (kipétʹ) (causative inchoative and causative continuative))
parole.testo: Derived from the same root as кипе́ть (kipétʹ, “to boil”), from Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English covet and hope.

parole.significato: kisel, kissel (a popular jellied dessert made by cooking berry juice or other fruit juice with milk, flour and oatmeal,…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyselь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kys(ь)lъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kysnǫti. By surface analysis, кис(лый) (kis(lyj)) + -нуть (-nutʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kystь. Related to Polish kiść (“a bunch (of fruit, flowers, or other things)”), and to ки́та (kíta, “bunch, bouquet)”). See also Proto-Germanic *skauba- (“sheaf”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyta.

parole.significato: to put on airs; to boast, to brag
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic кычити (kyčiti), кычити ся (kyčiti sja), from Proto-Slavic *kyčiti, derivative of Proto-Slavic *kyka.

Possibly inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyšěti. Cognate with Ukrainian киші́ти (kyšíty), Belarusian кішэ́ць (kišécʹ). Related to Lithuanian kušė́ti (“to move”) and to Latvian kustēt and kušņāt (“to move”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyšьka.

parole.significato: to bow (to, before), to greet (to bend oneself as a gesture of respect or deference)
parole.testo: From dialectal кла́нять (klánjatʹ, “to make bow”) + -ся (-sja), inherited from Proto-Slavic *klaňati. Iterative of клони́ть (klonítʹ), with unexpected stress shift and root vowel lengthening.

parole.significato: to put, to lay, to lay down, to deposit
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klasti; compare Old Church Slavonic класти (klasti) (first-person singular кладѫ (kladǫ)), Ukrainian класти (klasty), Belarusian класці (klasci), Serbo-Croatian кла̏сти (first singular кла́де̄м), Slovene klásti (first singular kládem), Czech klást (first singular kladu),

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kľьvati. Compare Bulgarian кълва́ (kălvá), Belarusian клюва́ць (kljuvácʹ), Old Church Slavonic клюıѫ (kljuıǫ), Slovene kljuváti, Polish kluć, Ukrainian клюва́ти (kljuváty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klějь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klepati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic клѣтъка (klětŭka), from Proto-Slavic *klětъka, from *klětь / *klětъ.

parole.significato: the log walls framing and enclosing a room; cribbing
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klětь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klěščь. Cognate with кле́щи (kléšči).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klěšči (singular *klěšča). Cognate with клещ (klešč).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klìkati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klìknǫti. By surface analysis, кли́кать (klíkatʹ, “to call”) + -нуть (-nutʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klinъ.
From Proto-Slavic *klakъ (“tuft, clump”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to curl up, form into a ball”), see also Old High German klakka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klokotati.

Inherited from Old East Slavic клубъ (klubŭ), from Proto-Slavic *klǫbъ; cognate with Ukrainian клуб (klub), Czech kloub, Polish kłąb.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klǫbьnь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъlykъ. Cognate with коло́ть (kolótʹ). Compary typologically би́вень (bívenʹ) (< бить (bitʹ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kľuvъ, which is cognate with Proto-Slavic *kľunъ, whence Bulgarian клюн (kljun), Serbo-Croatian кљун, Slovene kljun.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kľuka.
Inherited from Old East Slavic клюсѧ (kljusę), from Proto-Slavic *kľusę.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kľučь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kljaukjas, from Proto-Indo-European *klewk-yo-s, from *kle(h₂)uk-, an extended form of *(s)kleh₂w- (“hook, key, peg”), whence English clef and close.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klęti. Cognates include Old Church Slavonic клѧти (klęti), Ukrainian клясти (kljasty), Bulgarian кълна (kălna), Serbo-Croatian клети, Czech klít, Polish kląć.

Inherited from Old East Slavic клꙗтва (kljatva), from Proto-Slavic *klętva (“a type of oath”), per Brückner derived from Proto-Slavic *kloniti (“to incline, bend”) due to touching the ground with a hand during this type of oath.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klęča, *klęčь.

Uspensky in the Fenya argot of Vladimir with the meaning 'noble' (provided клювый (kljuvyj) in the "Suzdal dialect" by Pallas in 1787 is a misprint or typo instead of *кліовый). parole.significato: scream, screech (of certain birds of prey)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klekotъ, from Proto-Slavic *klekati (whence Old East Slavic клекати (klekati), 1sg. клечꙋ (kleču)). Probably onomatopoeic in origin.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klenъ.

From Proto-Slavic *kъňižica.

By surface analysis, княг- (knjag-) + -ы́ня (-ýnja). князь (knjazʹ) is derived from Early Proto-Slavic *kuningu, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz, with з by the a

parole.significato: young prince (the son of a prince); a duke's son
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic кнѧжичъ (knęžičŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kъnęžiťь (“son of a prince”). By surface analysis, князь (knjazʹ) + -ич (-ič).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь, borrowed from Germanic, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz. The feminine form княги́ня (knjagínja, “princess”) has preserved the original, Germanic g sound. Doublet of ксёндз (ksjondz), a borrowing from Polish, and ко́нунг (kónung).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kobьcь.

From ко́б(ец) (kób(ec), “small hawk, Pernis apivorus (European honey buzzard)”) + -чик (-čik), from Proto-Slavic *kobьcь. Per Vasmer, probably cognate with English hawk, Old High German habuh (“hawk”), Old Norse haukr (“hawk”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kobyla.

Inherited from Old East Slavic кобꙑлъка (kobylŭka), from Proto-Slavic *kobylъka. By surface analysis, кобы́ла (kobýla) + -ка (-ka). parole.significato: augury, specifically through the flight of birds, ornithomancy
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic кобь (kobĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kobь. Cognate with Bulgarian коба (koba), прокоба (prokoba, “ill fate, portent”), Serbo-Croatian коб/kob (“fate”). Non-Slavic cognates include Old Norse happ (“good luck”), Old Irish cob (“victory”), English hap.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kovaľь. By surface analysis, кова́ть (kovátʹ) + -ль (-lʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kovàti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kovъkъ.

parole.significato: feathergrass (Any of various perennial hermaphroditic grasses of the genus Stipa)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kovylь, *kovylъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic когда (kogda), from Proto-Slavic *kogъda, from Proto-Slavic *koda, from which the following words also were derived: Old Church Slavonic къгда (kŭgda), Bulgarian кога (koga), Polish kiedy, gdy, Serbo-Croatian када / kada, Slovene kdaj, Czech kdy, Lower Sorbian gdy. Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kogъtь, from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *keng- (“peg; hook”). Compare Belarusian ко́каць (kókacʹ), Ukrainian коготь (kohotʹ), кіготь (kihotʹ), когіть (kohitʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koža. By surface analysis, коза́ (kozá) + Proto-Slavic *-ja. Compare typologicalyy мех (mex), мешо́к (mešók) (<< Proto-Indo-European *moysós); овчи́на (ovčína) (<~ овца́ (ovcá)); лоси́ны (losíny) (< лось (losʹ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kožuxъ. By surface analysis, ко́жа (kóža, “leather, skin”) + -ух (-ux).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koza.
From Proto-Slavic *kozьjь. By surface analysis, коза́ (kozá) + -ий (-ij).
Inherited from Old East Slavic козьлъ (kozĭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kozьlъ (“he-goat”), from *koza (“she-goat”) + *-ьlъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic къи (kŷi), from Proto-Slavic *kъjь (“who, what, which”), from *kъ (“who”) + *-jь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kas (“who”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos (“who”).

From the Old East Slavic колбаса (kolbasa), from Proto-Slavic *kъlbasa.
Inherited from Old East Slavic колѣбати (kolěbati), from Proto-Slavic *kolěbati.

Inherited from Old East Slavic колеса (kolesa), plural of коло (kolo), from Proto-Slavic *kolo (oblique: *koles-), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlom (“circle”), *kʷékʷlos (“circle”) whence English wheel and cycle.

parole.significato: rut (mark of wheels on the ground)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolěja. Related to *kolo. Cognate with Bulgarian коловоз (kolovoz), Czech kolej, Polish koleina, Serbo-Croatian колотраг. Compare typologically Galician rodeira, rodal, rodada, rilleira, Spanish rodera (<… Latin rota).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolě.

parole.significato: what number, which (in a numbered series), how manyth
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic коликъ (kolikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kolikъ. Cognates include Old Church Slavonic коликъ (kolikŭ).
Most likely from ко́лоб (kólob, “a ball, a lump (dialectal)”) + -ок (-ok, “little thing”); then inherited from Old East Slavic колобъ (kolobŭ), possibly, from Proto-Slavic *kolbъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolovortъ. Cognate with Belarusian калаўро́т (kalawrót) and Ukrainian коло́ворот (kolóvorot). Doublet of коловра́т (kolovrát).
Inherited from Old East Slavic колода (koloda), from Proto-Slavic *kolda.

Inherited from Old East Slavic колодязь (kolodjazĭ), from Proto-Slavic *koldędzь. Early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *kaldingaz, from Proto-Germanic *kaldiǭ, whence Old Norse kelda (“source”), Danish kilde (“source”), Finnish kaltio (“source”). Doublet of кла́дезь (kládezʹ), a borrowing from Old Ch
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koldьcь, from earlier *koldędzь (whence коло́дезь (kolódezʹ)) with change of suffix.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolkolъ.

parole.significato: ear (fruiting body of a grain plant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kȏlsъ. Related to коло́ть (kolótʹ).

parole.significato: to be in the ear, to form ears
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolsiti. By surface analysis, ко́лос (kólos) + -ить (-itʹ) + -ся (-sja)

parole.significato: to knock, to strike, to bang
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kōltìti.

parole.significato: to split, to cleave, to break (sugar), to crack (nuts), to chop (firewood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kòlti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolybělь. By surface analysis, колеба́ть (kolebátʹ) + -ель (-elʹ)

parole.significato: to rhythmically sway, to rock gently
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolyxati.

parole.significato: an extinct Christmas folk tradition, featuring people going around singing Christmas carols and receiving gifts
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolęda, from Latin kalendae. Doublet of кале́нды (kaléndy).

Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kolo. According to Vasmer, this word was documented in Old Russian since 1695 as каслика. It is cognate with Polish kolasa. By surface analysis, коло (kolo, “a wheel”) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolesьnъ. By surface analysis, колесо́ (kolesó) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komarъ.
Derived from Proto-Slavic *komъ. Related to ком (kom) and комо́лый (komólyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komolъ (“hornless, mutilated”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic конъ (konŭ, “limit”), from Proto-Slavic *konъ (“beginning; end”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic коньць (konĭcĭ, “end; edge, border”), from Proto-Slavic *konьcь (“end”), from *konъ (“beginning; end”) + *-ьcь, from *čęti (“to begin”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic коньчьнꙑи (konĭčĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *konьčьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьnica. By surface analysis, конный (konnyj) + -ица (-ica).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьnъ. By surface analysis, конь (konʹ) + -ный (-nyj).
Dialectally vocalized also коно́пля, which is probably the original stress of Proto-Slavic *konopľa (“hemp”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic коното́пъ (konotópŭ), from Proto-Slavic *konotòpъ (“swamp in which the horse drowned”). Cognate with dialectal Belarusian канато́п (kanatóp, “swamp, bog, marsh”).
Possibly from Proto-Slavic *konotòpъ (“plants trampled by horses”). Cognate with dialectal Ukrainian коното́п (konotóp, “knotweed; red clover”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьskъ. Equivalent to конь (konʹ) + -ский (-skij)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konura. Compare Mongolian хонуурь (xonuurʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьčina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьčiti. By surface analysis, коне́ц (konéc) + -ить (-itʹ). Cognates include Belarusian ко́нчыць (kónčycʹ), Ukrainian кінчи́ти (kinčýty), Polish kończyć, Czech končit.

parole.significato: groom, stableman, hostler (person at an inn who looks after horses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic конюхъ (konjuxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *koňuxъ. By surface analysis, конь (konʹ) + -ух (-ux).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koňušьna. By surface analysis, ко́нюх (kónjux) + -ня (-nja).

parole.significato: sixty pieces of something (e.g. eggs, cucumbers, sheaves of hay or rye, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopa.
Inherited from Old East Slavic копати (kopati), from Proto-Slavic *kopati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kop-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to strike, beat”).

parole.significato: to accumulate, to gather, to amass
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic копити (kopiti, “to amass, to gather, e.g. people for an army”), from Proto-Slavic *kopiti (“to stack, to pile, e.g. hay”), from *kopa (“heap, pile”), from *kopati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kop-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to strike, beat”)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopъtь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopъtiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopylъ.

parole.significato: hazelwort (Asarum europaeum, the genus Asarum and also other species in it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic копытникъ (kopytnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kopytъnikъ. By surface analysis, копы́то (kopýto) + -ник (-nik).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopyto, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. For the relation with копа́ть (kopátʹ), compare typologically Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (órux). For the relation with копьё (kopʹjó), compare typologically Ancient Greek ὁπλή (hoplḗ), ὅπλον (hóplon).

Inherited from Old East Slavic копие (kopije), from Proto-Slavic *kopьje (see details of derivation there), from *kopati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kop-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to strike, beat”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кора (kora, “bark”), from Proto-Slavic *kora (“bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic корабль (korablĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korabľь, see more there. The marijuana sense is by consonance with коробо́к (korobók, “small box”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kory.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrzьno.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korìti. Compare Old East Slavic кор (kor, “swearword, offence”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic корица (korica), from Proto-Slavic *korica, diminutive of Proto-Slavic *kora (“tree bark”). Cognates include Ukrainian кори́ця (korýcja), Belarusian кары́ца (karýca).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кърмъ (kŭrmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kъrmъ.

parole.significato: stern (rear end of a ship or other vessel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrma.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic коробъ (korobŭ), from Proto-Slavic *korbъ (“basket”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korbiti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to turn”). Likely related to Proto-Slavic *krǫpъ (“concise, compact”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic коробъка (korobŭka), from Proto-Slavic *korbъka. By surface analysis, ко́роб (kórob) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korva; related to English horn and hart (“male red deer”), Welsh carw (“deer”) and Latin cervus (“deer”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic король (korolĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korľь. Doublet of Карл (Karl). Compare typologically царь (carʹ), це́сарь (césarʹ) (akin to Це́зарь (Cézarʹ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korsta.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korstělь. Cognate to Bulgarian кра́стел (krástel), Czech chřástal, Old Church Slavonic крастѣль (krastělĭ) and Polish chruściel.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kortati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ. Doublet of кра́ткий (krátkij), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: to work hard/meticulously/thoroughly (on something), to pore over, to plug away
parole.testo: Related to корпа́ть (korpátʹ, “to mend clothes, to patch”), from Proto-Slavic *kъrpati (“to patch”), from Proto-Slavic *kъrpa (“a patch, a cloth”), via semantic shift: to patch → to work → to work hard, to pore over. Related to Ukrainian ко́рпати (kórpaty, “to dig”), Serbo-Croatian krpati (“to patch

parole.significato: to uproot, to root out, to extirpate (to pull up by the roots)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrčevati, related to корч (korč, “stub, stump of a tree”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrčiti. By surface analysis, ко́рча (kórča) + -ить (-itʹ).

parole.significato: tavern, inn where spirits are sold (in Ukraine or Belarus before the Russian Revolution)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kъrčьma.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koristьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kȍrystь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koryto.
Per Vasmer, possibly from Proto-Slavic *kóry. Cognate with Ukrainian кір (kir).

parole.significato: braid, plait, tress, pigtail, queue (of hair)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic коса (kosa), from Proto-Slavic *kosa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kositi.

parole.significato: mane; disheveled locks; matted hair, mop
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kosmъ.

parole.significato: slanting, oblique, skewed (inclined at an angle to the plane; not straight, not sheer)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kosъ. Per Vasmer, derived from коса́ (kosá, “plait, braid”). Cognate with Ukrainian ко́сий (kósyj), Serbo-Croatian ко̑с, Czech kosý, Polish kosy.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kostьnъ. By surface analysis, кость (kostʹ) + -ный (-nyj)
Inherited from Old East Slavic кость (kostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kostь. Compare Latin costa, whence English coast and English costa (“rib-like structure”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kostrъ.

From the earlier form козу́ля (kozúlja), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *koza (“goat”), referring to the similarity in build and eye shape. Compare to the derivation of Latin capreolus (“a small roe deer, roebuck”) from Latin capra (“she-goat”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic котъ (kotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kotъ. Should be separated from коти́ться (kotítʹsja) (related to око́т (okót), catulus), the connection with this word is secondary.
Inherited from Old East Slavic которꙑи (kotoryi), from Proto-Slavic *kotorъjь, *koterъjь, definite of **kotorъ, **koterъ, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷóteros.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kotьlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kočanъ. (head): Compare typologically ре́па (répa), ты́ква (týkva), ты́ковка (týkovka).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кочьтъ (kočĭtŭ), ultimately from a suffixal form of Proto-Slavic *kokotъ; compare Belarusian ко́чат (kóčat), Polish koczot.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *košara.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *košelь from *košь.

Inherited from Middle Russian ко́шка (kóška), from Old East Slavic ко́шька (kóšĭka), from unattested *ко́чька (*kóčĭka), from Proto-Slavic *kòťьka, from *kòťь, from *kòtъ. Cognate with Old Ruthenian ко́шка (kóška), Ukrainian кі́шка (kíška).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kraďa.

parole.significato: krajina (used in the names of regions, a krajina is one of the regions inhabited mostly by Serbs in the former Yugoslav…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krajina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krajь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krajьnъ. By surface analysis, край (kraj) + -ний (-nij).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopriva, *kropiva. This is an instance in which the vowel reduction о (o) → а (a) is reflected in spelling: the expected spelling is кропи́ва (kropíva).
Inherited from Old East Slavic краса (krasa), from Proto-Slavic *krasa.

parole.significato: to color, to paint, to dye
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic красити (krasiti) from Proto-Slavic *krasiti; the original sense was “to decorate”, as in Slavic cognates like Old Church Slavonic красити (krasiti), Polish krasić, Czech krášlit, Bulgarian крася́ (krasjá), Macedonian краси (krasi). Compare sense development to кра́ска

Inherited from Middle Russian кра́ска (kráska), from Old East Slavic *кра́съка (*krásŭka), from Proto-Slavic *kràsъka, from *krāsà. краса́ (krasá, “beauty”) + -ка (-ka), first attested in the 15th century; original sense is hypothesized to be “blush” or “decoration”. Compare sense development to кра

Inherited from Old East Slavic красьнъ (krasĭnŭ), красьнꙑи (krasĭnyi, “beautiful, good”), from Proto-Slavic *krasьnъ (“beautiful”). The sense “red” is unique to Russian and did not develop in other Slavic descendants of *krasьnъ; first attested in 1515 in Muscovite diplomatic correspondence, it serv
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krasti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kremy.

parole.significato: kremlin (a central fortress in medieval Russian cities)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic кремль (kremlĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kremľь, probably related to Proto-Slavic *kroma (“edge”) (referring to the fortifications).

parole.significato: to fasten, to secure in place, to timber, to support, to prop
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěpiti. By surface analysis, кре́пкий (krépkij) + -ить (-itʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěpъkъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic крѣпость (krěpostĭ, “strength”), from Proto-Slavic *krěpostь, from *krěpъ (“strong”) + *-ostь. Senses related to fortification attested since 16th-17th centuries. Possibly influenced by German Festung (“fortress”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěpъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěslo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krьstiti. Compare кстить (kstitʹ), with different treatment of the reduced vowel.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krečetъ, perhaps of imitative Proto-Indo-European origin (see Ancient Greek κρέξ (kréx, “corncrake”)). Compare Ancient Greek κέρκνος (kérknos, “a Hierax or an Alektryon”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кривьда (krivĭda), from Proto-Slavic *krivьda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krivъ.

parole.significato: cry (a shout or scream), outcry, scream, shout, shouting, yell
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krȋkъ.

parole.significato: to cry, to shout, to scream, to yell
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kričati. By surface analysis, крик (krik) + -а́ть (-átʹ, stative).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кровъ (krovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *krovъ (“roof”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъvavъ, from *kry.

parole.significato: roofing, roof covering, rooftop (the outer surface of a roof)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krovlja (*-ja is suffix), correlative with *kroviti, *kryti (“to cover, hide”), *krovъ (“roof”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъvьnъ. By surface analysis, кровь (krovʹ) + -ный (-nyj).

Inherited from Old East Slavic крꙑ (kry), from Proto-Slavic *kry, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krū́ˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood of a wound”). Cognate with Latin cruor (“blood(shed)”), Lithuanian kraujas, Welsh crau, English raw.

parole.significato: to cut out (fabric to specific lengths and shapes to make clothes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krojìti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кромѣ (kromě, “outside”), old locative case of крома́ (kromá, “partition”), from Proto-Slavic *kroma (“edge, boundary”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kromъka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kropiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kropotьlivъ. By surface analysis, кропота́ть (kropotátʹ, “to grumble; to fuss, to bustle”) + -ли́вый (-lívyj).

parole.significato: loom (usually with some work on it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krosno.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъtъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кротъкъ (krotŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *krotъkъ. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian кро̀так / kròtak.
From Old East Slavic кръха (krŭxa), from Proto-Slavic *krъxa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krušā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *krows-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кръхътьнъ (krŭxŭtĭnŭ), from кръхъть (krŭxŭtĭ, “crumb, speck”), from Proto-Slavic *krъxa. See кро́ха (króxa).

parole.significato: to cut into small pieces, to chop, to crumble
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъšiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫglъ. By surface analysis, круг (krug) + -лый (-lyj). Compare Old Church Slavonic крѫглъ (krǫglŭ), Ukrainian кру́глий (krúhlyj), Bulgarian кръ́гъл (krắgăl), Serbo-Croatian окру́гао, Slovene krógǝl, Czech okrouhlý, Polish krągły.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫgovortъ.

parole.significato: to turn, to whirl, to spin, to wheel around
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫžiti or круг (krug) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krupa, from Proto-Indo-European *krowpeh₂.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krupьnъ. By surface analysis, круп(а) (krup(a)) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: to twist, to twirl, to roll up
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫtъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krušiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kridlo. Ы probably appeared by the influence of крыть (krytʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kridlьce from *kridlo (“wing”) + *-ьce (“diminutive suffix”). By surface analysis, крыло́ (kryló) + -цо́ (-có).

Uncertain. Hypotheses include: * an alteration of a term related to грызть (gryztʹ, “to gnaw, to nibble”) – compare to грызу́н (gryzún, “rodent”); * cognate with крот (krot, “mole”); * from Proto-Slavic *krysъsa (“blood-sucker”). Cognate with Ukrainian кри́са (krýsa).

parole.significato: to cover, to roof (a house); to thatch, to tile
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kryti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic *крꙑша (*kryša), from Proto-Slavic *kryša, from *kryti (“to cover, hide”) + *-ša (< *-sja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kręžь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krьstъ. Compare крест (krest), a Church Slavic borrowing.
Inherited from Old East Slavic къто (kŭto), from Proto-Slavic *kъto, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷós.

Inherited from Old East Slavic кубъ (kubŭ, “drinking vessel”), first attested in the 14th century, further origin uncertain. Cognate with Ukrainian куб (kub, “wooden dish”), Polish kubek (“bowl, cup”), Lower Sorbian kub (“bowl, cup”), also kubk. Per Vasmer, likely related to Sanskrit कुम्भ (kumbha,

Apparently related to кувы́рдать (kuvýrdatʹ, “to throw a stick”), кувы́рдаться (kuvýrdatʹsja, “to tumble”). Per ESSJa (Trubachev), from Proto-Slavic *kuvьrtati, formed from a prefix *ku- + the root of *vьrtěti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кѫда (kǫda), from Proto-Slavic *kǫda.
From Old East Slavic кѫдѣль (kǫdělĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kǫdělь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кудесъ (kudesŭ, “magic, sorcery”), from Proto-Slavic *kudo.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кудити (kuditi, “to decry; to insult; to spoil”), from Proto-Slavic *kùditi, from *kudъ / *kudь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫdrь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кудрꙗвꙑи (kudrjavyi), from Proto-Slavic *kǫdřavъ, from *kǫdrь + *-avъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic коузньць (kuznĭcĭ), from коузнь (kuznĭ) + -ьць (-ĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kuznьcь. Distantly related to кова́ть (kovátʹ), кова́ль (koválʹ) and the equivalent forms in other Slavic languages, such as Ukrainian кова́ль (koválʹ), Polish kowal, Czech kovář, Slovak kováč, S
Inherited from Old East Slavic кузница (kuznica), from кузнь (kuznĭ, “forging”) + -ица (-ica); compare Polish kuźnica. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ku- (“to forge”).

parole.significato: to cringe, to shrivel, to curdle
parole.testo: Ultimately from old dialectal Russian ку́ка (kúka, “a hook”), in turn from Proto-Slavic *kuka (“hook, hook-shaped”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫkoľь, *kǫkolъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kulikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kumъ, back-formation from *kuma (“godmother”), from Balkan Vulgar Latin *cómmater, from Latin compater (“godfather”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kucъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ladъ, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: boat, longship (a type of medieval vessel propelled by oars and a sail)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oldī, cognate with modern Russian ло́дка (lódka).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *làziti.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olkomъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *làska (“caress”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lasica ~ *laska.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lebeda or *elbeda. Doublet of лобода́ (lobodá), лабуда́ (labudá), бала́нда (balánda), ала́бута (alábuta), and ала́бота (alábota).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *elbedь, *elbędь, *olbǫdь, from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьvъ, likely a borrowing from a Germanic language, ultimately from Latin leo.
From лево́й (levój) (accent alignment – from пра́вый (právyj) – in pairs closely related in meaning) from Old East Slavic лѣвъ (lěvŭ, “left, wrong, evil”), from Proto-Slavic *lěvъ.
лёгкий (ljóxkij) + -о (-o), from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *leděnъ.

parole.significato: to lie (to be in a horizontal position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ležati, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.

parole.significato: to climb (up, on to), to scramble
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти (lězti), from Proto-Slavic *lězti (“to crawl, climb”).

parole.significato: doctor, medico, physician (feminine form "ле́карша" is usually considered colloquial)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěkařь. Was the official name of the profession in Russian Empire.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lemexъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lišajь.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lobъzati.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lomiti.

parole.significato: the inner bark of a tree, bast

from Old East Slavic лукъ (lukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lǫkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lankás, from Proto-Indo-European *lenk- (“to bend”). Cognate with Lithuanian lankas.

parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic луна (luna, “moon”), from Proto-Slavic *luna (“moon”).

parole.significato: rather, would better (do something) (often used with verbs in the past tense with subjunctive бы (by))

parole.significato: ski (one of a pair of long flat runners designed for gliding over snow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lyža, if existing in Proto-Slavic at all. Cognate with Ukrainian ли́жа (lýža).
Inherited from Old East Slavic лꙑко (lyko), from Proto-Slavic *lyko (“bast”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lúnˀkan (“bast”).
