Inherited from Proto-Slavic *morьskъ. By surface analysis, мо́ре (móre) + -ско́й (-skój), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri, whence English marine and maritime.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъrščina. Compare Belarusian маршчы́на (marščýna), Czech mrština, Old Church Slavonic мръщина (mrŭština), Ukrainian морщина (morščyna).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъrščiti. Compare Bulgarian мръ́щя (mrắštja), Czech smrsknout, Slovene mŕščiti, Old Church Slavonic съмърсканъ (sŭmŭrskanŭ), Polish marszczyć, Ukrainian мо́рщити (mórščyty).

parole.significato: seaman, sailor, mariner (a member of the crew of a vessel; a person experienced in nautical matters)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *mořakъ (by surface analysis, мо́ре (móre, “sea”) + -я́к (-ják)), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri, whence English marine and maritime.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мостъ (mostŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mostъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mastás.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *motati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *motovidlo.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мотыка (motyka), from Proto-Slavic *motyka, cognate to Latin mateola (“implement for digging in the soil”), English mattock.

parole.significato: moth (the small variety that swarms at night)
parole.testo: From a diminutive of Proto-Slavic *motyľь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъxъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *músos.
Inherited from Old East Slavic моча (moča), from Proto-Slavic *moča / *močь (“wetness, puddle, urine”), from *mok- + *-ja, *-jь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mok-.

parole.significato: to wet, to moisten, to douse, to humidify
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *močiti. Cognates include German machen, Ancient Greek μάσσω (mássō), Latin mācerō, Lithuanian makonė. (to kill, to waste): Compare typologically топи́ть (topítʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moťi, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-. Cognate to Ancient Greek μῆχος (mêkhos, “means, remedy”) and Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”) (whence English may, might).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moťь, from Proto-Indo-European *mógʰtis, *megʰ- (“to allow, be able, help”). Cognate to Proto-Germanic *mahtiz and its descendants like English might. Doublet of мощь (moščʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: midge (a kind of gnat or gnatlike fly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъši. Related to му́ха (múxa).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mošьna, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mak- (“small (leather) bag or pouch”), see also Lithuanian mãkas, Old High German maga, German Magen (“stomach”).

parole.significato: to avenge, to revenge, to retaliate (to take vengeance)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьstiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫdo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫdrьcь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫdrostь. By surface analysis, му́дрый (múdryj) + -ость (-ostʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic мудръ (mudrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mǫdrъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mandras, from Proto-Indo-European *mondʰh₁ros, from *men(s)dʰh₁- + *-rós. Cognate with Lithuanian mandrùs and Proto-Germanic *mundraz (German munter).
Inherited from Old East Slavic мѫжь (mǫžĭ), from Proto-Slavic *mǫžь, from Proto-Indo-European *mon-, whence English man.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫžьskъ. By surface analysis, муж (muž, “man”) + -ско́й (-skój).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǭka (“flour”). Akin to regional Serbo-Croatian мука/muka (“meal”), Slovene moka, Slovak múka. Non-Slavic cognates include Ancient Greek μάσσω (mássō, “to knead”), German and Old High German mengen (“to mix”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫka (“torment, torture”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mura, cognate with Proto-Slavic *murъ and further with Lithuanian mauras.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *murava, from *mura, *murъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mauˀras (“mud”). Cognate with Polish murawa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *morvьjь, from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫtiti (“to stir, trouble”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫtьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mùxa.

parole.significato: to torment, to anguish (cause to suffer pain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mǫ̀čiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъčati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мꙑ (my), from Proto-Slavic *my. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic мꙑ (my). Also akin to Lithuanian mẽs and Old Armenian մեք (mekʻ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mydlo, from *myti (“to wash”). By surface analysis, мыть (mytʹ) + -ло (-lo). For the term and помо́и (pomói) relation with мыть (mytʹ), compare typologically Ancient Greek ῥύμμα (rhúmma) < ῥύπτω (rhúptō, “to cleanse, to wash”). Also compare σμῆμα (smêma) < σμάω (smáō). A
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mysliti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *myslь. Cognate with Polish myśl, Macedonian мисла (misla), Bulgarian мисъл (misăl), Slovene misel, Serbo-Croatian мисао or misao, Czech mysl.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *myto.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *myti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *myti sę, reflexive of Proto-Slavic *myti. Cognate with Bulgarian мия (mija), Serbo-Croatian мити, Czech mýt, Polish myć; and with Lithuanian maudyti, Latvian maut.

From Proto-Slavic *mỳšь (“mouse”) (referring to the mouse-like appearance of a flexing muscle), from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s. For semantic development, compare to Latin mūsculus (“muscle”, literally “little mouse”) and Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse; muscle”).
From Old East Slavic мꙑшь (myšĭ), from Proto-Slavic *myšь (“mouse”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mū́ˀšis, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. The computing term is a semantic loan from English mouse.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мѧкъкъ (mękŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *minˀkakas, from Proto-Indo-European *mn̥k-o-kó-s, from *menk-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mękyna.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mę̀knǫti.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męso, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms. Compare Serbo-Croatian meso, Czech maso, Polish mięso, and Slovene meso. Compare Old Prussian mensa (“meat”). Sense 5 refers to the football club being supported by a meat factory in Moscow during the 1930s.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męta, borrowed from Latin menta (“mint”), from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).

parole.significato: to rumple, to crumple, to wrinkle, to fumble, to crease
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męti; compare Old Church Slavonic мѧти (męti).

parole.significato: ball (object, generally spherical, used for playing games)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męčь, related to мя́гкий (mjáxkij). Cognate with Ukrainian м'яч (mʺjač), Belarusian мяч (mjač), Czech míč, Slovene mȇč.

PIE word  *médʰu From Old East Slavic медъ (medŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mȅdъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *médu, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu. Cognate with English mead, Ancient Greek μέθυ (méthu, “wine”) (whence Russian мети́л (metíl), English methyl).
Inherited from Old East Slavic мерзлꙑй (merzlyj), from Proto-Slavic *mьrzlъ. By surface analysis, мёрз(нуть) (mjórz(nutʹ)) + -лый (-lyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьrznǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьrtvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós, ultimately from the root *mer- (“to die”), whence also English murder, mortal, morbid and French mourir.
Inherited from Old East Slavic на (na), from Proto-Slavic *na, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en-.

parole.significato: here you go! (encouraging someone to accept something, used when giving or providing something, i.e., "take it!", "here…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *na.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *na.

parole.significato: to set up, to compose, to type (a text on a computer)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nabirati. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + -бира́ть (-birátʹ).

parole.significato: set, kit, outfit, collection (collection of various objects for a particular purpose, such as a set of tools)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naborъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *navykъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic наглъ (naglŭ, “quick”), from Proto-Slavic *naglъ. Per Vasmer, cognates include Sanskrit अञ्जसा (añjasā, “soon, suddenly”), अञ्जस् (añjas, “instantly, quickly”) and Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌺𐍃 (anaks, “suddenly”).
Inherited from Middle Russian на́глый (náglyj), from Old East Slavic на́глꙑи (náglyi), на́глъ (náglŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nãglъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nagъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked”); see there for the cognates.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nagrěvъ, from *grěvъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic надъ (nadŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nadъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naděja.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nadějati sę. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + де́ять (déjatʹ) + -ся (-sja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nadъzorъ. Cognate with надзира́ть (nadzirátʹ, “to supervise”). See Proto-Slavic *nadъ and *zьrěti for more information.
Inherited from Old East Slavic надо (nado), надобѣ (nadobě), from dative/locative singular of надоба (nadoba), from Proto-Slavic *nadoba, from *na- + *doba.
Inherited from Old East Slavic надоба (nadoba), from Proto-Slavic *nadoba (whence Czech nádoba (“dish, container”)), from *na + *doba (whence Old Church Slavonic доба (doba, “use, advantage”)).
Inherited from Old East Slavic надежа (nadeža), from Proto-Slavic *nadeďa. Doublet of наде́жда (nadéžda) borrowed from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nadeďьnъ. By surface analysis, надёжа (nadjóža) + -ный (-nyj)

parole.significato: prefix forming superlatives from comparative adjectives (or nonstandardly from positive adjectives)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *najь-. Compare Ukrainian най- (naj-), Polish naj-, Serbo-Croatian naj-, Slovak naj- Slovene naj-, Czech nej-, Macedonian нај- (naj-), Bulgarian най- (naj-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *najьti (“find”). By surface analysis, на- (na-) + -йти́ (-jtí). Cognates include Ukrainian знайти́ (znajtý), Belarusian знайсці́ (znajscí).
From Proto-Slavic *nakazъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naklonъ. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + клони́ть (klonítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naličьnъ. By surface analysis, на (na) + лицо́ (licó) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nalogъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *napastь. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + пасть (pastʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *napisati. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + писа́ть (pisátʹ, “to write”). Cognate with Latin pingō (whence English paint and picture), and with Persian نوشتن.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *napitъkъ. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + пить (pitʹ) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naporъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *napьrstъkъ. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + перст (perst, “finger”) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *narězati. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + ре́зать (rézatʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *narěčьje. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + речь (rečʹ) + -ие (-ije).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nareťi. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + -речь (-rečʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *narodъ. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + род (rod).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *narodьnъ. By surface analysis, наро́д (naród) + -ный (-nyj).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naročьnъ. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + рок (rok, “fate, destiny”) + -ный (-nyj) + -о (-o). Compare Old Church Slavonic нарочьнъ (naročĭnŭ), Bulgarian нарочно (naročno), Polish naroczny.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ružь. Cognate with Latvian raugs, raudzīt.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *narušiti. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + ру́шить (rúšitʹ). Compare Polish naruszyć.
Inherited from Old East Slavic насилиѥ (nasilije), from Proto-Slavic *nasilьje.

parole.significato: to force, to coerce, to constrain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic насиловати (nasilovati), from Proto-Slavic *nasilovati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic насильникъ (nasilĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nasilьnikъ.

parole.significato: to jump [with на (na, + accusative) ‘into a fence, etc.’] while on horseback
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naskakati. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + скака́ть (skakátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nasъlati. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + слать (slatʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nastrojь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nauka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naučьnъ. By surface analysis, нау́ка (naúka) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naxalъ.

parole.significato: to begin, to start, to commence
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic начѧти (načęti), from Proto-Slavic *načęti. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + -чать (-čatʹ), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“new, fresh”), whence English recent and ceno-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic нашь (našĭ), from Proto-Slavic *našь.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ne, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ne, from Proto-Indo-European *né. Cognates include Lithuanian ne, Old English ne, German nicht, nie, Gothic 𐌽𐌹 (ni), Irish ní, Latin ne, Sanskrit न (ná).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nevědomъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic невѣжа (nevěža), from Proto-Slavic *nevěďa (“ignorant person < ignorance”), from *ne- + *věďa, from *věděti (“to know”). Doublet of неве́жда (nevéžda).
From Proto-Slavic *nevěrьnъ. By surface analysis, не- (ne-) + ве́рный (vérnyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nevěsta.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nevidimъ. By surface analysis, не- (ne-) + ви́димый (vídimyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nevodъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nevoľa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *něga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *negodějь. Can also be analysed as не (ne) + годи́ться (godítʹsja, “to be of good use”) + -яй (-jaj)

Inherited from Old East Slavic недѣлꙗ (nedělja, “Sunday”), from Proto-Slavic *neděľa (“Sunday”). By surface analysis, не- (ne-, “not”) + де́л- (dél-, “work”) + -я (-ja). Originally used to mean Sunday, the day of rest.

parole.significato: lack, deficiency, deficit, shortage (an insufficient quantity)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *nedostatъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nědra.

parole.significato: disease, illness, malady (an abnormal condition of the body causing discomfort or dysfunction)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nedǫgъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *něžiti. By surface analysis, не́га (néga) + -ить (-itʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *něžьnъ. By surface analysis, не́га (néga, “luxury, comfort, prosperity”) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: it is impossible (perfective aspect), one cannot, you can't
parole.testo: From не (ne) + льзя (lʹzja), from Old East Slavic нельзѣ (nelĭzě), нельзѧ (nelĭzę), нельза (nelĭza), from Proto-Slavic *ne / *ně + *lьga (“possibility”) (possibly influenced by its dative *lьdzě), likely related to *lьgъkъ (whence лёгкий (ljóxkij, “light, easy”)). Compare Ukrainian не́льга (nélʹha),
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *něměti. By surface analysis, немо́й (nemój) + -е́ть (-étʹ)

Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣ́мьць (ně́mĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *němьcь (“foreigner, German”), from *němъ (“mute”) (whence Russian немо́й (nemój)). Compare typologically Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros), whence ва́рвар (várvar).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *němьčьskъ, from Proto-Slavic *němьcь. By surface analysis, не́мец (némec) + -цкий (-ckij), from немо́й (nemój, “mute”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *němъ. Compare Old Church Slavonic нѣмъ (němŭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *němota.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nenaviděti. Cognates include Old Church Slavonic ненавидѣти (nenaviděti), Belarusian ненаві́дзець (njenavídzjecʹ), Ukrainian нена́видіти (nenávydity), Polish nienawidzić, Serbo-Croatian nenávidjeti, Czech nenávidět, Slovak nenávidieť, and Bulgarian ненави́ждам (nenavížda
Inherited from Old East Slavic ненависть (nenavistĭ), from Proto-Slavic *nenavistь, from *nenaviděti + *-tь, from *ne (“not”) + *naviděti, from *na (“on(to), in(to)”) + *viděti (“to see”).
Derived from Proto-Slavic *narokъ (analysable as не- (ne-) + на- (na-) + рок (rok, “fate”) + -ом (-om, adverbial suffix)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nepogoda. Compare Czech nepohoda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nepravьda. By surface analysis, не- (ne-, “un-”) + пра́вда (právda, “truth”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *neprijateľь. By surface analysis, не (ne) + прия́тель (prijátelʹ). For the word formation compare Latin inimīcus (in- + amīcus), whence enemy. Also compare не́друг (nédrug) (не- (ne-) + друг (drug)).
From Old East Slavic нерестъ (nerestŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nerstъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nérśtas.

parole.significato: to bear, to bring, to carry
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic нести (nesti), from Proto-Slavic *nestì.
From не- (ne-) + Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьnъ. By surface analysis, не- (ne-) + сча́стье (sčástʹje) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣту (nětu), Proto-Slavic *nětu, from *ne (“not”) + *e, short form of *estь (“is”) + *tu (“there, here”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *netopyřь, a compound which first part nekto- (e-grade) is cognate to Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (o-grade).

parole.significato: Constantly burning, inextinguishable; unrelenting, permanently existing.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *neugasimъ. By surface analysis, не- (ne-) + у- (u-) + га́снуть (gásnutʹ) + -ый (-yj)
From Proto-Slavic *neudobьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *něčьto. Morphologically from не- (ne-) + что (što).

parole.significato: tawny owl (Strix, a genus of owls)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nejęsytь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ни (ni), from Proto-Slavic *ni.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ňiva.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nikъde.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nižьjь, from *niz- + *-ьjь. See Russian низ (niz).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizъ, from Proto-Indo-European *nei-ǵʰ-? (Derksen) or *ni- (“down”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizati. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian ни́зати (1sg. ни̑же̄м), Slovene nízati (tonal orthography) (1sg. nȋžem, nȋzam (tonal orthography)), Bulgarian ни́жа (níža), Church Slavonic низати (nizati), Polish nanizać, Lower Sorbian nizaś. Related to Proto-Slavic *nьziti; compare
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ni-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *niknǫti. Slavic cognates include Czech vzniknout (“to arise, originate”) and Serbo-Croatian niknuti (“to sprout, spring”). Further cognates include Ancient Greek νεῖκος (neîkos, “quarrel, strife”) and Ancient Greek νῑ́κη (nī́kē, “victory”).

parole.significato: nobody, no one; (with negative) anybody, anyone
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic никъто (nikŭto), from Proto-Slavic *nikъto. By surface analysis, ни- (ni-) + кто (kto).
From Old East Slavic нить (nitĭ), from Proto-Slavic *nitь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nī́ˀtis, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ничьто (ničĭto), from Proto-Slavic *ničьto. By surface analysis, ни- (ni-, “not”) + что́ (štó, “what”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *niščeta. By surface analysis, ни́щий (níščij) + -ота́ (-otá).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *niščь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nъ, from Proto-Indo-European *nu. Cognate with English now and Latin num ("now") and nunc (< *num + ce, "now").
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nòvъ, related to English new and novel.
Inherited from Old East Slavic нога (noga), from Proto-Slavic *noga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nogъtь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-, *h₃nogʷʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nožь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nozdra.

parole.significato: now, nowadays, today, currently (as opposed to the past)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *nъně.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nora.
Inherited from Old East Slavic норовъ (norovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *norvъ. Doublet of нрав (nrav).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nosatъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nosačь (“big-nosed man/animal”), from *nosъ (“nose”) + *-ačь. By surface analysis, нос (nos, “nose”) + -ач (-ač).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nositi, iterative form of *nesti (whence also нести́ (nestí)).

parole.significato: a kind of tub used for performing household jobs, particularly bathing small children and kneading dough
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночьвы (nočĭvy), from Proto-Slavic *nъťьvy.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ночьлѣгъ (nočĭlěgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *noťьlěgъ. By surface analysis, ночь (nočʹ, “night”) + лежа́ть (ležátʹ). Compare Ukrainian нічлі́г (ničlíh), Belarusian начле́г (načljéh), Polish nocleg, Czech nocleh, Slovak nocľah.

parole.significato: night, nighttime (period of time from sundown to sunup)
parole.testo: PIE word  *nókʷts Inherited from Old East Slavic ночь (nočĭ), from Proto-Slavic *noťь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *náktis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Doublet of нощь (noščʹ, “night (archaic)”), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nu.

Inherited from Old East Slavic нꙋдити (nuditi), from Proto-Slavic *nuditi. Cognate with Ukrainian нуди́ти (nudýty), Belarusian нудзі́ць (nudzícʹ), Old Church Slavonic ноудити (nuditi, “to force, to compel”) and нѫдити (nǫditi) (per Vasmer, with secondary nasalization), Bulgarian ну́дя (núdja, “to fo
Inherited from Old East Slavic нужа (nuža), inherited from Proto-Slavic *nuďa. Doublet of нужда́ (nuždá), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: the inside, the inward nature (especially of a person), gut feeling
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫtro.
Inherited from Old East Slavic нꙑнѣ (nyně), from Proto-Slavic *nyně, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”), compare with Ukrainian ни́ні (nýni), German nun, English now.
Derived from Old East Slavic нꙑнѣ (nyně) (whence ны́не (nýne)), from Proto-Slavic *nyně, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nyrnǫti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. Compare Old Church Slavonic нирıати (nirıati), Belarusian ны́рка (nýrka), Bulgarian ни́рна (nírna).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nyřati. By surface analysis, нырну́ть (nyrnútʹ) + -я́ть (-játʹ).

parole.significato: to whimper, to whine, to yammer, to snivel, to bellyache, to cry (to complain peevishly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nyti (“to yearn”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ňuxъ, itself of uncertain origin.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ňuxati.

From Proto-Slavic *ňaňa, a reduplicated nursery formation. Similar nursery formations are widespread in Proto-Indo-European; compare Sanskrit नना (nanā́, “mother”), Ancient Greek νάννα (nánna, “aunt”), Albanian nënë (“mother”), Welsh nain (“grandmother”). The related form ня́нька (njánʹka) was first
From Old East Slavic небо (nebo), from Proto-Slavic *nebo, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *nébas, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos. Doublet of не́бо (nébo), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Old East Slavic о (o), from Proto-Slavic *o, ultimately a natural expression. Compare Ancient Greek ὦ (ô), Latin ō.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi.

parole.significato: prefix added to adjectives or nouns to produce factitive verbs in conjunction with -ить (-itʹ), i.e. verbs with the mea…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ab, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi.
Inherited from Old East Slavic оба (oba), from Proto-Slavic *oba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóh₁, whence also Lithuanian abù, Latvian abi, Latin ambo, Ancient Greek ἄμφω (ámphō).

Inherited from Old East Slavic оба дъва (oba dŭva), from Proto-Slavic *oba dъva. By surface analysis, univerbation of оба (oba) + два (dva). Compare Italian ambedue, Romanian amândoi, Polish obydwa, Serbo-Croatian obadva.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ob(ъ)turъ, *ob(ъ)tura, from the verb *ob(ъ)turiti. Compare *turiti (“to chase, drive away”). Related to отурить, отурять (oturitʹ, oturjatʹ, “capsize, confuse, deceive”). According to Anikin, the word's age renders unlikely the Turkic etymology proposed by Vasmer, who de

parole.significato: lunch, dinner (the main meal of the day, which is served between noon and 3 p.m.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obědъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic обѣдати (obědati), from Proto-Slavic *obědati, from *obědъ + *-ati, ultimately from *ěsti (“to eat”). By surface analysis, обе́д (obéd, “dinner, lunch”) + -ать (-atʹ, “infinitive suffix”). See also объеда́ть (obʺjedátʹ).
Derived from оберега́ть (oberegátʹ), and then бере́чь (beréčʹ), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *berťi.
Inherited from Old East Slavic обѣчати (oběčati), from Proto-Slavic *oběťati. Doublet of обеща́ть (obeščátʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obzorъ. By surface analysis, deverbal from обозре́ть (obozrétʹ), with typical Indo-European nominal o-vocalism (compare набо́р (nabór) and набра́ть (nabrátʹ), the latter with future tense наберу́ (naberú) etc. showing typical Indo-European present/future verbal e-vocalis
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obvida, from *obviděti, from *ob- + *viděti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obilьje. Cognate with Czech obilí (“grain, cereals”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obilъ. By surface analysis, оби́лие (obílije) + -ный (-nyj)

parole.significato: to pick, to collect (from a tree or garden)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obirati. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + -бира́ть (-birátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obixodъ. By surface analysis, оби- (obi-) + ход (xod).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oblava.

parole.significato: face, look, aspect, appearance, figure, image
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oblikъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic обличье (obličĭje), from Proto-Slavic *obličьje, from *oblikъ + *-ьje, from *ob- + *likъ. Cognate with Belarusian аблі́чча (ablíčča), Ukrainian обли́ччя (oblýččja). By surface analysis, о́блик (óblik) + -ье (-ʹje).

parole.significato: boot (part of a carriage where the coachman sits)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic облукъ (oblukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *oblǫkъ, from *lǫkъ (“bow”) (akin to *lęťi). Compare typologically Proto-Germanic *bankiz (whence English bench, Russian ба́нка (bánka) (via German Bank), банке́тка (bankétka)) (< Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obьlъ, from Old East Slavic обьлъ (obĭlŭ).

parole.significato: faint, swoon, syncope (the act of fainting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obmorkъ, from *o(b) + *morkъ
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obvodъ.

parole.significato: string of carts, wagon train, string of sledges
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obozъ. By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + воз (voz). Compare cognate Polish obóz (“camp”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obvonjanьje.

parole.significato: cords with which bast shoes are fastened to the foot
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obora (“string, twine”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bornь. Related to брань (branʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obvortiti, a derivative of *vortiti. By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + вороти́ть (vorotítʹ). Doublet of обрати́ть (obratítʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Old East Slavic *объсьрати (*obŭsĭrati), from Proto-Slavic *o(b)sьrati. By surface analysis, обо- (obo-) + сра́ть (srátʹ).

By surface analysis, обою́ду (obojúdu, “on both sides”) + -ный (-nyj), the former from Old East Slavic обоѭдоу (obojǫdu) (by surface analysis, о́ба (óba) + -ю́ду (-júdu), the latter suffix from Proto-Slavic *-ǫdu).

Inherited from Old East Slavic образъ (obrazŭ), from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ. By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + раз (raz). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic образъ (obrazŭ), Ukrainian о́браз (óbraz), Polish obraz.
From Proto-Slavic *obrokъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic обручь (obručĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obrǫčь (“wrist, bracelet, ring”), from *ob + *rǫka (“arm, hand”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obrędъ.

parole.significato: to put shoes on someone's feet, to help someone put on his/her shoes
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic обувати (obuvati), from Proto-Slavic *obuvati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic обувь (obuvĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obuvь. By surface analysis, обува́ть (obuvátʹ) + -ь (-ʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic обузъ (obuzŭ), from Proto-Slavic *obvǫzъ, *obvǫza. Compare Old Church Slavonic обѫзъ (obǫzŭ).

parole.significato: to put shoes on someone's feet, to help someone put on his/her shoes
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obuti. By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + -уть (-utʹ).

parole.significato: butt (the thicker end of a tool or a weapon, especially an axe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic обухъ (obuxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *obuxъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic обьчии (obĭčii), from Proto-Slavic *obьťь. Doublet of о́бщий (óbščij), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obъjězdъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obъjętьje. By surface analysis, объя́ть (obʺjátʹ) + -тие (-tije)

From об- (ob-) and Proto-Slavic *jęti (“to take”). Compare German Umfang (“extent, scope”) from umfangen (“to embrace, to include”), which is regarded as a calque of Latin circumferentia from Greek περιφέρεια (periféreia).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obyknovenъ. By surface analysis, обыкнове́ние (obyknovénije) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obyčajь, from *vyknǫti (whence -вы́кнуть (-výknutʹ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *obyčьnъ, from *obyťi (*o(b)- + *vyťi) and *obyknǫti (*o(b)- + *vyknǫti) + *-ьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ovьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *awinas.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jevinъ.

parole.significato: gadfly, botfly (an insect of genus Oestrus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ovadъ.
From Old East Slavic врагъ (vragŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ. Compare Bulgarian овра́г (ovrág).

parole.significato: sheep (a domestic sheep of either gender)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic овьца (ovĭca), from Proto-Slavic *ovьca, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *áwis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis. See also English ewe and ovine, Latin ovis.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ovьsъ, which is a cognate with Latin avena.

parole.significato: place where there was a fire (with ashes and charcoals)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic огнище (ognišče), from Proto-Slavic *ogňišče.
By surface analysis, оголте́ть (ogoltétʹ, “to go crazy”) + -лый (-lyj), from Proto-Slavic *gъltati.

Inherited from Old East Slavic огнь (ognĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ogňь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ugnis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis. Cognate with Latvian uguns, Latin ignis (whence English ignition and igneous, Latin borrowings), Sanskrit अग्नि (agní). Compare also Hittite 𒀀𒀝𒉌𒅖 (a-ak-ni-iš), an
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic, from Proto-Slavic *odeďa. Doublet of одёжа (odjóža), the inherited East Slavic form.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oděti. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + деть (detʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic одинъ (odinŭ), единъ (jedinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *edinъ. Doublet of един- (jedin-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *odolěnъ (“valerian”).

parole.significato: to overcome, to overpower, to conquer
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic одолѣти (odolěti), from Proto-Slavic *odolěti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic одръ (odrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *odrъ.
Inherited East Slavic form of Proto-Slavic *odeďa. Doublet of оде́жда (odéžda), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)žerdlьje. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + жерело́ (žereló, “mouth, muzzle, throat; opening”) + -ье (-ʹje). Cognates include Bulgarian огърлица (ogărlica), Serbo-Croatian огрлица, Czech náhrdelník, Slovak náhrdelník.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ožidati. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + -жида́ть (-židátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ob zemь, the latter part an alternative form of *zemľa (“earth, land”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic озеро (ozero), from Proto-Slavic *ȅzero, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *éźeran.
From Proto-Slavic [Term?]. Akin to Russian позо́р (pozór), зазо́рный (zazórnyj), озира́ться (ozirátʹsja).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *okъno. Related to Russian о́ко (óko, “eye”). For semantic parallels, compare Old English ēagþȳrel (“window”, literally “eye-hole”) and Old Norse vindauga (“window”, literally “wind-eye”) (whence English window).
Inherited from Old East Slavic око (oko), from Proto-Slavic *oko, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-.

parole.significato: shackles, manacles, gyves, fetters, irons (paired wrist or ankle restraints)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *okovъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *okolo, from *kolo.
Inherited from Old East Slavic окорокъ (okorokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *okorkъ, from *ob- + *korkъ (“leg”).

parole.significato: outskirts (the edges or areas around a city or town)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)krajina. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + край (kraj) + -ина (-ina) Proper noun sense is a mockery of Украи́на (Ukraína) to reflect Russian nationalist views depicting Ukraine as an outlying part of Russia.

parole.significato: outskirts; marginal, peripheral (relating to or located at the outskirts or margins)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)krajinьnъ. By surface analysis, окра́ина (okráina) + -ный (-nyj)
Inherited from Old East Slavic округъ (okrugŭ), from Proto-Slavic *okrǫgъ, from *ob- + *krǫgъ (“circle”).

parole.significato: to dip, to plunge (something into something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *okǫpnǫti. For the п (p) dropping, compare тону́ть (tonútʹ) (< Proto-Slavic *topnǫti, akin to *topiti (whence топи́ть (topítʹ))).
Inherited from Old East Slavic о́кунь (ókunĭ), from Proto-Slavic *òkunь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic олъ (olŭ, “fermented liquor; strong drink”), from Proto-Slavic *ȍlъ (“beer; fermented liquor”). Doublet of эль (elʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *elỳ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic олово (olovo, “lead, tin”), from Proto-Slavic *olovo (“lead, tin”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic оловѧнꙑи (olovęnyi), оловѣнꙑи (olověnyi), from Proto-Slavic *olověnъ, *olověnьnъ, from *olovo (“lead”) + *-ěnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olьxa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élis-. Compare Serbo-Croatian јо́ха, jóha.

parole.significato: inula, elecampane (Inula spp., especially Inula helenium)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *omanъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oměgъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *emela.

parole.significato: third-person masculine singular pronoun: he, it.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic онъ (onŭ), from Proto-Slavic *onъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *anas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos (“that”). Inflected forms from Old East Slavic и (i), from Proto-Slavic *jь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *is, from Proto-Indo-European *ís and Proto-Indo-European *Hyós. See
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ona.

Inherited from Old East Slavic они (oni), from Proto-Slavic *onъ. The prefixation of /n/ after prepositions comes from Proto-Slavic prepositions such as *sъ(n) (“with”) (compare Ancient Greek σύν (sún) and Latin cum), that originally ended in *-n and governed oblique cases. Since the prepositions an
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ono.
Inherited from Old East Slavic онъ (onŭ, “that, yonder”), from Proto-Slavic *onъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *anas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos (“that”). See он (on).

parole.significato: back, backwards, the other way round
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic опако (opako), from Proto-Slavic *opakъ (“the other way round”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)pasьnostь. By surface analysis, опа́сный (opásnyj) + -ость (-ostʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)pasьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)peka, a calque of Latin prōcūrātor. Compare Czech рéčе, Ukrainian опі́ка (opíka).

parole.significato: to be guardian to, to be trustee to, to have the wardship (of); to be warden to
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opekati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opekunъ, from *peťi. By surface analysis, опека́ть (opekátʹ) + -ун (-un).

parole.significato: gaize, marlstone (a hard, porous sedimentary rock with a high silica content)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)poka. Compare Polish opoka, Czech opuka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)pora.
Inherited from Old East Slavic опорознити (oporozniti), from Proto-Slavic *oporzdьniti.

parole.significato: to justify, to warrant, to authorize, to vindicate
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opravьdati. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + пра́вда (právda) + -ать (-atʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic опꙑтъ (opytŭ), from Proto-Slavic *o(b)pytъ, from *obpytati, from *ob- + *pytati (“to ask, examine”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opętь. Cognates include Czech opět and Serbo-Croatian opet.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oradlo. By surface analysis, ора́ть (orátʹ) + -ло (-lo).
Inherited from Old East Slavic орати (orati), from Proto-Slavic *oràti. Cognate to Lithuanian árti, Latin arō, Ancient Greek ἀρόω (aróō).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orěxъ. Compare Albanian arrë (“walnut”), Ancient Greek ἄρυα (árua, “walnut”), Latvian riẽksts, Serbo-Croatian òrah.
From Old East Slavic орьлъ (orĭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orьlъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *arélis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃érō.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *osa, from Proto-Indo-European *wobʰseh₂.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)sada.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b)sadъ with ending -ок (-ok). Related to сад (sad) and сажать (sažatʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *osьla or *osla̋, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-l-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic осла (osla), Slovak osla, Slovene ósla, Polish osełka. More distant cognates include Armenian ասեղ (aseġ, “needle”) and dialectal German Achel (“awn”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic осень (osenĭ), from Proto-Slavic *esenь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-en-, whence English earn and German Ernte (“harvest”). Doublet of есень (jesenʹ) and есеня (jesenja), cognate with Belarusian во́сень (vósjenʹ) and Ukrainian о́сінь (ósinʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opsina, *opsa, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)osp-eh₂, from *(H)osp-. Cognates include Ukrainian оси́на (osýna), Belarusian асі́на (asína), Lithuanian ẽpušė, Latvian apse, Old Prussian abse and Proto-Germanic *aspō.
From Old East Slavic основа (osnova), from Proto-Slavic *osnova.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *osobьnъ. By surface analysis, осо́бый (osóbyj) + -енный (-ennyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic осътъ (osŭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *osъtъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic осъпа (osŭpa), from Proto-Slavic *osъpa; related to сы́пать (sýpatʹ), сыпь (sypʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ostatъkъ. By surface analysis, оста́ться (ostátʹsja) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ostoržьnъ. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + сто́рож (stórož) + -ный (-nyj)
From Old East Slavic остриѥ (ostrije), from Proto-Slavic *ostrьje.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ostroga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ostrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ostь.

Inherited from Old East Slavic робота (robota), from Proto-Slavic *orbòta. By surface analysis, роби́ть (robítʹ) + -о́та (-óta). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic работа (rabota), whence spelling. Doublet of ро́бот (róbot).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orbotati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orbotьnikъ, from *orbotьnъ + *-ikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orbotęga. By surface analysis, рабо́тать (rabótatʹ, “to work”) + -я́га (-jága).

parole.significato: worker (a person who performs physical labor for hire, especially in industry, construction, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orboťь, from *orbota + *-jь. By surface analysis, рабо́та (rabóta) + -ий (-ij).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orbьskъ, from *orbъ (“slave, servant”) + *-ьskъ. By surface analysis, раб (rab) + -ский (-skij).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orbьstvo, from *orbъ + *-ьstvo. Also analyzable as раб (rab) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: plain (an expanse of land with relatively low relief)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orvьnina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *radъ.
From Proto-Slavic *raditi.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *radi.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *radostьnъ. By surface analysis, ра́дость (rádostʹ) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic радость (radostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *radostь. By surface analysis, рад (rad) + -ость (-ostʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *radǫga. The first element more likely derives from Proto-Slavic *radъ (“glad, dear, willing”) than folk etymology’s Proto-Slavic *rajь. Compare Russian весёлка (vesjólka, “rainbow”) (dialectal) related to весёлый (vesjólyj, “merry, cheerful, happy, convivial, gleeful, li

Inherited from Old East Slavic разъ (razŭ, “strike”), from Proto-Slavic *razъ. Akin to рази́ть (razítʹ), ре́зать (rézatʹ). For a different semantic shift, compare Polish raz. Compare typologically Proto-Slavic *brojiti, *brojь (akin to *briti, whence брить (britʹ), << Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH-).

Inherited from Old East Slavic роз- (roz-), from Proto-Slavic *orz-. The spelling "раз-" was reinforced by Old Church Slavonic раз- (raz-), as well as vowel reduction, which is also reflected in Belarusian раз- (raz-).

parole.significato: analysis, review, critique, investigation, examination, inquiry
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzborъ.

Parallel to and possibly borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раздражити (razdražiti). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian дра́жити (“to pester, to anger”) (1sg. дра̑жим), Slovene drážiti (“to pester”), Old Czech drážiti, Slovak dráżiť. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *dražiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orz(ъ)zěvati. By surface analysis, разе́- (razé-) + -ва́ть (-vátʹ)

parole.significato: gawk, gaper, scatterbrain (a distracted, inattentive, clumsy person)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orz(ъ)zěva.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orz(ъ)zinǫti, from *orz- + *zinǫti. Cognate with Belarusian разіну́ць (razinúcʹ), Serbo-Croatian razinuti, Bulgarian раззи́на (razzína), Macedonian раззине (razzine).

parole.significato: to strike, to hit, to smite
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *raziti. Cognate to ре́зать (rézatʹ). (to reek (of), to stink (of)): Compare typologically English stink (<< Proto-Indo-European *stengʷ-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzměrъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic разорити (razoriti), from Proto-Slavic *orzoriti, from *orz- + *oriti. Compare Old Church Slavonic разорити (razoriti), Serbo-Croatian разо̀рити, Old East Slavic разорь (razorĭ), Old Church Slavonic орити (oriti).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzuti. By surface analysis, раз- (raz-) + -уть (-utʹ). Compare with Polish rozzuć.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rajь, borrowed from Iranian, from Proto-Iranian *raHíš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *raHíš, from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rakъ.

parole.significato: sallow, willow (Salix fragilis, Salix caprea) (tree or wood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orkyta, which Pokorny connects to Ancient Greek ἄρκευθος (árkeuthos, “juniper”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷ- (“bend”). Also compare Latvian ērkšķis (“thorn bush”).

parole.significato: shell (hard calcareous external covering of mollusks)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic раковина (rakovina, “mother of pearl”). Per Vasmer, from Proto-Slavic *orky (“shell”) (genitive *orkъve) + *-ina, from Proto-Germanic *arkō (“chest, coffer”), from Latin arca (“chest, coffer, coffin”). Cognate with ра́ка (ráka, “shrine of a saint, originally coffin”),
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ordlo, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ormę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rana.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ranenъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *raniti, from *rana.
From Proto-Slavic *ranъ + -о (-o).

parole.significato: to unwind, to unroll, to unspin
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic разкрꙋтити (razkrutiti), from Proto-Slavic *orzkrǫtiti. Morphologically рас- (ras-) + крути́ть (krutítʹ).

parole.significato: dissolute, libertine, profligate, dissipated, immoral, lecherous, wanton, rakish, reprobate, abandoned, wicked, self-ab…
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *orzpustьnъ, equivalent to распусти́ть (raspustítʹ) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Middle Russian разсвѣтъ (razsvět), from Old East Slavic *розсвѣтъ (*rozsvětŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orzsvětъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzsolъ. By surface analysis, рас- (ras-) + сол (sol). Cognate with Polish rosół.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orztvorъ. By surface analysis, deverbal from растворя́ть, раствори́ть (rastvorjátʹ, rastvorítʹ, “to dissolve”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orsti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er-.

parole.significato: to grow, to raise, to cultivate
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orstiti.

parole.significato: to cancel, to dissolve, to annul, to abrogate
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orztъrgati (“to tear away, to rip apart”), from *orz- (“un-, apart, away”) + *tъrgati (“to tear, to rip”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzčьtъ, from *čisti; synchronically analyzable as a deverbal form of рас- (ras-) + -читать (-čitatʹ).

parole.significato: cleft, crevice, fissure (narrow crack in rock or ice)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščelina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ortьnikъ. By surface analysis, рать (ratʹ) + -ник (-nik)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ortьnъ. By surface analysis, рать (ratʹ) + -ный (-nyj)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ortovati. By surface analysis, рать (ratʹ) + -овать (-ovatʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ortь. Related to реть (retĭ, “quarrel, competition”). Cognates include Sanskrit ऋति (ṛti, “assault”), Sanskrit ऋतीयते (ṛtīyate, “to quarrel, to hate”), Sanskrit समरण (samaraṇa, “war, strife”), Ancient Greek ἔρῐς (érĭs, “strife, quarrel”) and Proto-Germanic *ernustuz (see
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *račiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ръвати (rŭvati), from Proto-Slavic *rъvàti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ръдѣти сѧ (rŭděti sę), from Proto-Slavic *rъděti.
From Old East Slavic ребро (rebro), from Proto-Slavic *rebrò, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rébran, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ-.

parole.significato: child, kid, baby: children, kids, babies
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic робѧ (robę), diminutive of робъ (robŭ, “slave”) from Proto-Slavic *orbę. Compare with па́робок (párobok, “lad”) (dialectal). The relationship with "slave" could arise from the meaning "orphan" because orphans carried out the hard work in the household.

parole.significato: to roar, to bellow, to howl
parole.testo: Infinitive modified by analogy with 1sg. реву́ (revú), from Old East Slavic рюти (rjuti), from Proto-Slavic *řuti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rьvьnivъ. By surface analysis, ревнова́ть (revnovátʹ) + -и́вый (-ívyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic рьвьность (rĭvĭnostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rьvьnostь. By surface analysis, ре́вный (révnyj) + -ость (-ostʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rědъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *redьky.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězъ. Cognate with Czech řez, Polish rzeź.

parole.significato: to cut up, to cut open, to slice, to carve
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic рѣзати (rězati), from Proto-Slavic *rězati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rḗˀźtei, from Proto-Indo-European *wreh₁ǵ-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic рѣзати (rězati), Ukrainian різати (rizaty), Bulgarian режа (reža), Serbo-Croatian резати, Slovene rezati, Czech řezat, Slovak rezať,

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězvъ. Akin to ре́зать (rézatʹ). Compare typologically: Russian как ужа́ленный (kak užálennyj) (< ужа́лить (užálitʹ)), как ошпа́ренный (kak ošpárennyj) (< ошпа́рить (ošpáritʹ)), зада́ть стрекача́ (zadátʹ strekačá) akin to стрека́ть (strekátʹ).

parole.significato: cutter, cutting tool, chisel, draw knife
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězьcь. By surface analysis, рез(ать) (rez(atʹ), “to cut”) + -ец (-ec).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězъka. By surface analysis, ре́зать (rézatʹ) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězьba.
Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣка (rěka), from Proto-Slavic *rěka, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃royHkeh₂, from *h₃reyH-, whence English runlet and rivulet and Spanish río.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *remy (genitive *remene). Cognate to Old East Slavic ремыкъ (remykŭ), Old Church Slavonic ремень (remenĭ), Ukrainian ремінь (reminʹ); Bulgarian ремен (remen), ремик (remik), ремък (remăk); Serbo-Croatian ре̏ме̑н (genitive ремена), рѐмик; Slovenian rémen, jérmen; Czech řem
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *remeslo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rěpa. (head): Compare typologically ты́ква (týkva), ты́ковка (týkovka), коча́н (kočán), German Birne, Rübe, Italian zucca, Swedish knopp.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rěpьjь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣсьнъ (rěsĭnŭ) + -ица (-ica), from Proto-Slavic *ręsьnica, from *ręsa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rěčь (“speech”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic решето (rešeto) or рѣшето (rěšeto), from Proto-Slavic *rešeto.

Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣшити (rěšiti, “to untie, absolve”), from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti, from Proto-Indo-European *wreyḱ- (“to twist, bend”). Cognates include Ukrainian ріши́ти (rišýty), Belarusian рашы́ць (rašýcʹ), Serbo-Croatian решити, Czech řešit.

parole.significato: to soar, to fly, to hover
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣяти (rějati), from Proto-Slavic *rějati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ръжа (rŭža), from Proto-Slavic *rъďa.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ръжавъ (rŭžavŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъďavъ, from *rъďa + *-avъ. By surface analysis, ржа (rža) + -а́вый (-ávyj).
Inherited Old East Slavic ръзати (rŭzati), from Proto-Slavic *rъzati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewǵ-. Cognate with Czech ržát.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *riza.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rìnǫti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic робити (robiti), from Proto-Slavic *orbiti.

parole.significato: shy, timid, bashful (lacking in courage or confidence)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic робъ (robŭ, “serf”) + -кий (-kij), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic ровъ (rovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rovъ (“ditch, pitch”), from *ryti (“to dig”) (whence рыть (rytʹ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ. Cognate with Belarusian ро́ўны (równy). Doublet of ра́вный (rávnyj), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rogъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rágas. The irregular plural рога́ (rogá) is an old dual form.
From Proto-Slavic *rogatъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rogačь, from *rogъ (“horn”) + *-ačь. By surface analysis, рог (rog, “horn”) + -ач (-ač).
Inherited from Old East Slavic рогожа (rogoža), from Proto-Slavic *rogoža, from *rogozъ (“reed, rush”). By surface analysis, рого́з (rogóz) + Proto-Slavic *-ja.

parole.significato: bulrush, cattail (any of several wetland herbs, Typha)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rogozъ.

parole.significato: generation, birth, origin, stock, family, race, tribe, lineage
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic родъ (rodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *radás. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”), whence English root. Cognates include Latvian rads, Ukrainian рід (rid) and Polish ród amongst others.
From Proto-Slavic *rodina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rodìti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *roďa, related to *rodъ. Compare Old East Slavic рожаи (rožai, “appearance, face”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic ражати (ražati), from Proto-Slavic *raďati. Doublet of рожда́ть (roždátʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *roďanica. By surface analysis, род (rod) + -еница (-enica)

Inherited from Old East Slavic рожьство (rožĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *roďьstvo (“birth; birthday; Christmas”). Compare рожство́ (rožstvó). Doublet of Рождество́ (Roždestvó), a Church Slavic loanword.

parole.significato: pointed stake (placed at an angle in a defensive fortification)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oržьnъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic рожьство (rožĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *roďьstvo. Compare рожество́ (rožestvó). Doublet of Рождество́ (Roždestvó), a Church Slavic loanword.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ръжь (rŭžĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъžь. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian raž, Bulgarian ръж (răž), Latvian rudzi, German Roggen, English rye.

parole.significato: Stressed equivalent of раз- (raz-). Found primarily in deverbal nouns and past passive participles.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orz-. Doublet of раз- (raz-), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rozga, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *razgā́ˀ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)resg-. Cognates include Latin restis, Old Armenian երագազ (eragaz). Compare typologically плеть (pletʹ) akin to плести́ (plestí).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzьnъ. Doublet of ра́зный (ráznyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orz-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic рои (roi), from Proto-Slavic *rojь (“stream, current”). Compare cognate Old East Slavic нарои (naroi, “assault, onset”), Macedonian порој (poroj), Czech zdroj (“source, resource”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rokъ (Modern Russian срок (srok)). Related to речь (rečʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic рокотъ (rokotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rokotъ. Probably related to *reťi.

parole.significato: to roar, to roll, to murmur
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic рокотати (rokotati), from Proto-Slavic *rokotati. Probably related to *reťi.
From ронить (ronitʹ), from Old East Slavic ронити (roniti), from Proto-Slavic *roniti. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian ро̀нити, Polish ronić.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ръпътъ (rŭpŭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъpъtъ, onomatopoeic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rosà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *rasā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orzkošь.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ростъ (rostŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orstъ. Synchronically derivable as deverbal from расти́ (rastí, “to grow”); note that stem-stressed forms of this verb begin with рос- (ros-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rъtъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *oršča, from earlier *orstja. Cognate to Russian рост (rost, “growth”) and расти́ (rastí, “to grow”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic рътуть (rŭtutĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rьtǫtь, possibly related to Lithuanian risti (“to roll”),.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫbaxa, from *rǫbъ. By surface analysis, рубъ (rub, “a piece of cloth”) + -аха (-axa).

parole.significato: to axe, to fell, to chop, to cut (with an axe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti. Compare Belarusian руба́ць (rubácʹ), Bulgarian ръ́бя (rắbja), Ukrainian руби́ти (rubýty), Czech roubit, Polish rąbać.

parole.significato: cutting (of wood e.g. with an axe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫbežь. Doublet of рубе́ж (rubéž), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. By surface analysis, руби́ть (rubítʹ) + -ёж (-jóž).

parole.significato: to reprimand, to abuse, to scold, to rail, to curse out, to swear
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫgati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ruda.
Inherited from Old East Slavic рудъ (rudŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rudъ. Compare to Ukrainian руди́й (rudýj), Czech rudý, Polish rudy.
Inherited from a colloquial form of Old East Slavic оружие (oružije), from Proto-Slavic *orǫžьje, from *orǫga / *orǫžь. Doublet of ору́жие (orúžije).
From Old East Slavic рѫка (rǫka), from Proto-Slavic *rǫka, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ránkāˀ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫkavъ. Compare typologically Latin manica (< manus), German Ärmel (< Arm).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫkavica.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rǫko(j)ętь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic румꙗнъ (rumjanŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ruměnъ, from earlier *rudměnъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *runo.

parole.significato: fair(-haired), blond(e), light brown (of hair), dirty blond
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic русъ (rusŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rusъ, from earlier *rudsъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰ-s-o-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ruxnǫti, from *rȗxъ (“movement”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ručьjь. Akin to Ukrainian руча́й (ručáj), Czech ručej, Polish ruczaj.

Inherited from Old East Slavic рꙋшити (rušiti, “to destroy”), from Proto-Slavic *rušiti. Cognate with Ukrainian ру́шити (rúšyty, “to move, to wiggle”), also руша́ти (rušáty), Belarusian ру́шыць (rúšycʹ, “to move, to wiggle”), Old Church Slavonic роушити (rušiti, “to destroy”), Bulgarian ру́ша (rúša,
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryba, further etymology uncertain.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rybařь. By surface analysis, ры́ба (rýba) + -а́рь (-árʹ) (ending-stressed variant) or from ры́ба (rýba) + -арь (-arʹ) (stem-stressed variant).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rybьjь. By surface analysis, ры́ба (rýba) + -ий (-ij)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rygati.

parole.significato: to sob, to blubber, to weep (to make noises while crying)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic рꙑдати (rydati), from Proto-Slavic *rydati. Compare Sanskrit रोदिति (roditi), रोदति (rodati).
Inherited from Old East Slavic рꙑжии (ryžii), from Proto-Slavic *ryďь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rūdʰ-yo-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic рыло (rylo), from Proto-Slavic *rydlo (“spade, snout”). Related to Polish ryj. Compare typologically German Rüssel.

Reflexive of ры́пать (rýpatʹ, “to spring, to fling (oneself)”), which, in its turn, is from Proto-Slavic *rypati (“to burrow; to tear”). Cognate with Czech rýpat, Polish rypać, Bulgarian ри́пам (rípam).
Inherited from Old East Slavic рискати (riskati), from Proto-Slavic *riskati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rysь, distantly related to English lynx.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryti, from Proto-Slavic *rūti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryxlъ. Related to ру́шить (rúšitʹ).

parole.significato: to grumble, to growl, to snarl (to make a low growling or rumbling animal noise)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryčati, *rykati. Onomatopoeic.
