parole.significato: to hew (with an axe), to make (something) by cutting with an axe
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тесати (tesati), from Proto-Slavic *tesàti (“to hew”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tesla / *teslo (“adze”), from Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ-dʰlo-, from *tetḱ-. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian те̏сла, Polish ciosła, Old Norse þexla (“axe”), Old High German dehsala (“axe, adze”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *těsniti (“to narrow, to squeeze”). By surface analysis, те́сный (tésnyj) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣснъ (těsnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *těsnъ (“narrow”). According to Václav Machek, it is related to Ancient Greek στενός (stenós, “narrow, tight”), thus making both derive from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣсто (těsto), from Proto-Slavic *těsto.

parole.significato: the father of one's wife; father-in-law
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьstь.

parole.significato: black grouse (game bird of genus Tetrao, of the family Tetraonidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tetervь.

Inherited from Old East Slavic тѧтива (tętiva), from Proto-Slavic *tętiva. A rare example when ѧ in the root becomes unstressed in the inherited term (and thus becomes е, not я, compare лека́ло (lekálo)).

parole.significato: to flow, to run, to stream, to move
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic течи (teči), from Proto-Slavic *teťi.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣшити (těšiti), from Proto-Slavic *těšiti. Cognate to ти́хий (tíxij, “quiet”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тина (tina), from Proto-Slavic *tīmnā or *tiňa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tisъ, of disputed origin.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тискати (tiskati), from Proto-Slavic *tìskati (“to press, squeeze”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tisnǫti (“to press, squeeze”). By surface analysis, ти́скать (tískatʹ) + -нуть (-nutʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тихъ (tixŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tixъ.

parole.significato: to quiet down, to become quieter
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tixnǫti. By surface analysis, ти́хий (tíxij) + -нуть (-nutʹ).

parole.significato: silence, quietness, hush (the lack of any sound)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic тишина (tišina), from Proto-Slavic *tišina. By surface analysis, ти́хий (tíxij) + -ина (-ina).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъkanь, derived from ткать (tkatʹ, “to weave”), from Proto-Slavic *tъkati, from Proto-Indo-European *trūk-, *trūg- (“to press, beat”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъkati. Cognates include Old Church Slavonic тъкати (tŭkati) and possibly Ancient Greek τύκος (túkos, “hammer, chisel”), τυκίζω (tukízō, “I polish (stone)”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъkačь. By surface analysis, ткать (tkatʹ, “to weave”) + -ач (-ač).

parole.significato: to poke, to jab, to stick, to prod
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъknǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъlěnъ.

parole.significato: to rot, to decay, to putrefy, to moulder
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьlěti.

Inherited from Old East Slavic тьло (tĭlo), from Proto-Slavic *tьlo, whence also Macedonian тло (tlo), Serbo-Croatian тло, Slovene tla (“floor”). Non-Slavic cognates include Latin tellūs (“the Earth”), Sanskrit तल (tala, “surface”), Old Irish talam (“earth”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьmiti. Compare тьма (tʹma), тёмный (tjómnyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tovarъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic товарищь (tovariščĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tovariščь, from *tovarъ + *-iščь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тогда (togda), from Proto-Slavic *togъda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *to že. Can be analyzed as тот (tot, “that”) + же (že).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tokъ.
From Proto-Slavic *tъkъmo. Cognate with Bulgarian тъкмо (tʺkmo, “just, exactly”), Macedonian токму (tokmu, “just, exactly”) and Serbo-Croatian такмен, takmen (“equal”). Related to точка (točka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *toliko. Related to то́лько (tólʹko).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тълкъ (tŭlkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ.

parole.significato: to push, to shove, to thrust
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тълкнути (tŭlknuti, “to push; to knock; to attack”), from Proto-Slavic *tьlknǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъlkovati (“to interpret”). By surface analysis, толк (tolk) + -овать (-ovatʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь, from Proto-Turkic *tilmač (compare Turkish dilmaç (“interpreter”)), from Proto-Turkic *til (“tongue”) (Turkish dil) + Proto-Turkic *-mač (“noun suffix”). Cognate with Macedonian толмач (tolmač), Slovene tolmač, Serbo-Croatian ту̀ма̄ч/tùmāč, Polish tłumacz (“tran
Inherited from Old East Slavic толокъно (tolokŭno), from Proto-Slavic *tolkъno, related to толо́чь (tolóčʹ, “to pound”).

parole.significato: to pound, to crush, to grind (to make smaller by breaking with a device)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *telťi (“to pound”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic тълпа (tŭlpa), from Proto-Slavic *tъlpa. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic тлъпа (tlŭpa), Bulgarian тълпа (tălpa), Czech tlupa (“band”) and further related to Polish tłum.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъlstъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъlšča.
From Proto-Slavic *toli. Cognate with Polish tyle. See то́лько (tólʹko).
Inherited from Old East Slavic толико (toliko), from Proto-Slavic *toliko.

parole.significato: to weary (with a rather negative intention), to torment, to torture, to languish
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic томити (tomiti), from Proto-Slavic *tomiti, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic томити (tomiti).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тънъкъ (tŭnŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tьnъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *topnǫti, from *topiti + *-nǫti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тонꙗ (tonja), from Proto-Slavic *topnь or *tорni̯а. Related to топи́ть (topítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъpati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-. Related to Old Church Slavonic тъпати (tŭpati), Proto-Hellenic *túpt͏̌ō, Latin stupeō.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *topìti (“to heat”). Related to Russian тёплый (tjóplyj, “warm”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *topìti (“to heat”) (same as Etymology 1).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *topìti (“to drown”).

parole.significato: poplar, cottonwood (any of various deciduous trees of the genus Populus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *topolь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic топоръ (toporŭ, “poleaxe”), from Proto-Slavic *toporъ. Further etymology is disputed.

parole.significato: footfall, tread, tramp, trample, stamp, stomp
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъpъtъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- or ultimately, onomatopoeic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъpъtati. By surface analysis, то́пот (tópot) + -ать (-atʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic търгъ (tŭrgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъrgovati. By surface analysis, торг (torg) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ).

parole.significato: to tread, to clear (a path or road) (by frequent walking or traveling)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *toriti (“to tread, to make way”). By surface analysis, тор (tor, “beaten path”) + -и́ть (-ítʹ). Cognate with Ukrainian тори́ти (torýty); further, inherited from Proto-Slavic *torъ and cognate with Ukrainian тор (tor, “rut”) (gen. sg. то́ру (tóru)), Serbo-Croatian то̑р (“
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьrkati.

parole.significato: game straps (at the back of a seat for tying game)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *torkъ.

parole.significato: to hurry, to hasten, to precipitate, to rush
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *torpiti. Vasmer adduces Ancient Greek τρέπω (trépō, “to turn”) (from the Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ-), and possibly Ancient Greek τέρπω (térpō) (Proto-Indo-European *terp-).

parole.significato: a person who is always in a hurry
parole.testo: From торопи́ться (toropítʹsja). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *torpъ.

parole.significato: to stick out, to protrude, to jut out
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *(s)tъrčati. Cognate with Polish sterczeć.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъska, which is perhaps related to то́щий (tóščij) or ти́скать (tískatʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic тътъ (tŭtŭ), reduplication of Proto-Slavic *tъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tas, from Proto-Indo-European *só, *séh₂, *tód (“this, that”). Cognate with Old Polish tet, Latvian tas, Lithuanian tas, ta, Sanskrit स (sá), Sanskrit तत् (tat), Old English se (whence English the

parole.significato: to sharpen, to hone, to whet
parole.testo: Follows from the diachronic convergence of Proto-Slavic *tъčiti (“to point, to sharpen”) from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewk- (“to hew”) and Proto-Slavic *točiti (“to stiffen”) from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tek- (“to rig, to fixate”). Morphologically, an iterative of Russian ткнуть (tknutʹ, “to poke”).

parole.significato: to emit, to exude (smell, light, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *točiti (“to drain”), causative of ток (tok, “current”) + -ить (-itʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *tъčьka. Cognate with Lithuanian tãškas.

Inherited from Old East Slavic тъчьнъ, тъчьнꙑи (tŭčĭnŭ, tŭčĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *tъčьnъ. By surface analysis, ты́кать, то́чка (týkatʹ, tóčka) + -ный (-nyj). Compare typologically German pünktlich < German Punkt (<< Latin punctus (p.p.p. of pungō), whence also English point, punctual, пунктуа́льн
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъščьnъ. Related to *tъska (“grief”). Compare Old Polish tesny (“upsetting, wistful, boring”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъščь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tuskjas, from Proto-Indo-European *tus-sḱ-yós, from *tews- (“to empty”), from *tew- (“to swell”). Cognate with Polish czczy, Lithuanian tùščias, Latvian tukšs, Vedic Sanskrit तुच्छ्य (tucchyá), Persian تهی (tohi).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trava (“grass”). Related to трави́ть (travítʹ, “to spoil or damage the grass”) and тере́ть (terétʹ, “to rub”). Possibly a cognate of Ancient Greek τρώγω (trṓgō, “I eat, devour”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic травьнъ (travĭnŭ, “May”), from Proto-Slavic *travьnъ. Cognates include Ukrainian тра́вень (trávenʹ, “May”), Belarusian тра́вень (trávjenʹ), Serbo-Croatian travanj (“April”). Related to Russian трава́ (travá, “grass, herb”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *traviti. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic травити (traviti), Ukrainian трави́ти (travýty), Serbo-Croatian trovati, Czech trávit, Slovak trávit᾽, Polish trawić (first singular trawię). Further cognate with Ancient Greek τρώω (trṓō, “to hurt”), τιτρώσκω (titrṓskō), τρύ̄ω (
From Proto-Slavic *travьnikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tratiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trьbuхъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trьvožьnъ. By surface analysis, трево́га (trevóga, “alarm, alert, anxiety”) + -ный (-nyj).

Inherited from Old East Slavic трепати (trepati), from Proto-Slavic *trepati. Cognate with Ukrainian трепа́ти (trepáty), Belarusian трепа́ць (trjepácʹ), Slovene trépati (first singular trẹ́pljem), Czech třepat, Slovak trepať, Polish trzepać, Upper Sorbian třepać, Lower Sorbian tśepaś, tśapaś. Furthe
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trepetъ. Compare Bulgarian тре́пет (trépet), Slovene trepèt, Polish trzpiot and Ukrainian тре́пет (trépet).

parole.significato: crack, crash, snap (sharp sound made when solid material breaks)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *trěskъ (“crack, bang”).

parole.significato: cod (marine fish of the family Gadidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic трѣска (trěska), треска (treska), from Proto-Slavic *trěska.
Perhaps from тре́скать (tréskatʹ) + -ся (-sja), from Proto-Slavic *trěskati, or from треск (tresk) + -ать (-atʹ) + -ся (-sja). The same root appears in тре́снуть (trésnutʹ) and треща́ть (treščátʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic треть (tretĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tretь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tretias.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trěščati. By surface analysis, треск (tresk) + -а́ть (-átʹ), with iotation. The same root appears in the related verbs тре́скаться (tréskatʹsja), тре́снуть (trésnutʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic трие (trije), from Proto-Slavic *trьje, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tríjes, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
Per Vasmer, possibly inherited from Proto-Slavic *tryzna. Compare Czech trýzeň (“torture”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tri *sъta.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic [Term?]. From the same root as Latin trahō according to Goryaev, which would be Proto-Indo-European *tregʰ-, whence English drag, treat, trace, and traction.

parole.significato: three (in a group together), three of them
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trojь.

parole.significato: path, trail (a trail for the use of, or worn by, pedestrians)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tropa. Akin to трепа́ть (trepátʹ). Compare typologically Ancient Greek τρίβος (tríbos) (< τρίβω (tríbō) << Proto-Indo-European *terh₁-, whence also тере́ть (terétʹ)). Also compare доро́га (doróga) (akin to дёргать (djórgatʹ), драть (dratʹ)). Also compare Latin rupta via
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trъstь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic труба (truba), from Proto-Slavic *trǫba. Noncognate with Russian трубаду́р (trubadúr).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trǫbiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic трудъ (trudŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trudъ, from Proto-Indo-European *trewd-, whence also English threat.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *truditi.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trudьnъ. By surface analysis, труд (trud) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trupъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trǫsъ (“earthquake, shaking”), from *tręsǫ (“I shake”). Akin to трясти́ (trjastí), тру́сить (trúsitʹ) and труси́ть (trusítʹ).

parole.significato: to shake off, to shake out
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trǫsiti. Cognate to трясти́ (trjastí), трус (trus).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trǫsiti. Cognate to трясти́ (trjastí), трус (trus).
Inherited from Old East Slavic трудъ (trudŭ, “tinder fungus”), from Proto-Slavic *trǫdъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trǫtъ. Cognate to German Drohne, Lithuanian trãnas, Latvian trans.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *truxlъ. By surface analysis, труха́ (truxá) + -ля́вый (-ljávyj). Related to Macedonian трул (trul), Serbo-Croatian труо, Slovene truhel and Slovak trúchlý.

The first part is from Proto-Slavic *tręsti (“shake”), while the second part is from Proto-Slavic *gǫzъ (“butt, rump”). Literally, “rump shaker” (because of the movements this bird does with its tail)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tręstì.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тугъ (tugŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tǫgъ (“hard, strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *tengʰ- (extension of Proto-Indo-European *ten-).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тѫда (tǫda), from Proto-Slavic *tǫda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tǫžiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тукъ (tukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tukъ.

parole.significato: [with dative ‘to whom?’] to tell lies or half-truths that benefit the self, to bullshit
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tuliti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tǫpiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тупъ (tupŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tǫpъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tȗrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tuskъ (“fog, darkness”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic туто (tuto), тутъ (tutŭ, “here; thereto; herewith”), ту (tu, “there; thereto; then; here, herewith”), from Proto-Slavic *tuto, *tu.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tǫxlъ, also found as Proto-Slavic *tъxlъ (as in dialectal то́хлый (tóxlyj, “rotten and foul-smelling”)), which may represent an earlier variant. Compare ту́хнуть (túxnutʹ, “to become rotten and foul-smelling”), Belarusian тхліць (txlicʹ, “to cause to spoil”), ту́хнуць (t

parole.significato: to go out, to die out, to wink out (of light, fire)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tuxnǫti. Related to туши́ть (tušítʹ).

parole.significato: to go bad, to spoil (of food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tǫxnǫti or *tuxnǫti, related to ту́хлый (túxlyj). Possibly related to Etymology 1.

From Old East Slavic туча (tuča), from Proto-Slavic *tǫča, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to contract”). Compare the Slavic Old Church Slavonic тѫча (tǫča), Ukrainian ту́ча (túča), Polish tęcza and the Non-Slavic Gothic 𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍈𐍉𐌽 (þeiƕōn) and Old Norse þéttr. Unrelated to Russian ту́чный
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tučьnъ. By surface analysis, тук (tuk) + -ный (-nyj). Unrelated to Russian ту́ча (túča) (which historically had nasal vowel ѫ (ǫ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tušiti.

parole.significato: to endeavor, to strive, to try (usually in vain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тъщатисѧ (tŭščatisę), from Proto-Slavic *tъščati.

parole.significato: second-person singular, nominative case: you, thou
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тꙑ (ty), from Proto-Slavic *ty, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic тꙑ (ty).

parole.significato: to poke, to prod, to jab, to thrust
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tykati (sę).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тꙑкꙑ (tyky), from Proto-Slavic *tyky. (head): Compare typologically ре́па (répa), коча́н (kočán).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тꙑлъ (tylŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tylъ (“back of the head, back”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тꙑнъ (tynŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tynъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tỳsęťa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tū́ˀsantis, from Proto-Indo-European *tuHsont-. Cognate with Ukrainian тисяча (tysjača), Serbo-Croatian тисућа, tisuća, Slovene tisoč, Czech and Slovak tisíc, Polish tysiąc. Akin to English thousand, Gothic 𐌸𐌿𐍃𐌿𐌽𐌳𐌹 (þūsundi), Lithuanian t
Inherited from Old East Slavic тьма (tĭma), from Proto-Slavic *tьma, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *timāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-.

parole.significato: draft/draught, pull, draw (in a pipe, tunnel, chimney)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тяга (tjaga), from Proto-Slavic *tęgъ or *tęga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tędzati, *tęgati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tęžestь. By surface analysis, тя́жкий (tjážkij) + -ость (-ostʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тѧжькъ (tęžĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tęžьkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *tingús, from Proto-Indo-European *tengʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tęželъ. Related to тя́жкий (tjážkij); see there for more.

parole.significato: to pull, to draw, to haul, to drag
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti.
Compare Proto-Slavic *tępati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tetę, presumably of expressive or nursery origin, cf. Ukrainian та́то (táto).

parole.significato: namesake (person, place or thing having the same name as another)
parole.testo: From тёза (tjóza) + -ка (-ka), ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *tьzъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *teplъ, from Proto-Indo-European *tep-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьrnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tesъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tetъka. By surface analysis, тётя (tjótja) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Old East Slavic тета (teta), from Proto-Slavic *teta. Compare Polish ciocia, Ukrainian цьо́ця (cʹócja), Belarusian цёця (cjócja).

parole.significato: the mother of one's wife; mother-in-law
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tьšča.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *u-

parole.significato: wretched, poor, poverty-stricken, squalid, miserable, sordid, beggarly
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ubogъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uvy, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wai. Cognate with English woe, Latin vae, Lithuanian vai̇̃, Sanskrit उवे (uvé), Hittite [script needed] (uwai), Persian وای (vây).
у- (u-) + Proto-Slavic *garъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ugoda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ugodìti; compare *godìti (“to please”). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + годи́ть (godítʹ), but годи́ть (godítʹ) no longer has its original meaning.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng- (“corner”).

parole.significato: coal (a black rock formed from prehistoric plant remains, composed largely of carbon and burned as a fuel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic угъль (ugŭlĭ) or угль (uglĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫglь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ánˀglis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óngʷl̥ (“charcoal”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic ѫгль (ǫglĭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫgořь.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫgrъ. Outside Slavic, cognate with Lithuanian ankštiras. It is not known whether the two senses of the word are cognate. Folk etymology suggests that a blackhead, when squeezed out, resembles an eel in its elongated form, hence the origin of the second sense.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъrinъ, Old East Slavic угринъ (ugrinŭ), plural угре (ugre), doublet of венгр (vengr) and уго́рец (ugórec) (dated or dialectal). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic ѫгринъ (ǫgrinŭ), plural ѫгре (ǫgre), Polish Węgier or Węgrzyn.
Verbal form of угро́за (ugróza, “threat, danger”), from гроза́ (grozá, “terror”), from Proto-Slavic *groza (“terror”) (vd. there for cognates)

parole.significato: threat (expression of intent to injure or punish another)
parole.testo: From гроза́ (grozá, “terror”), from Proto-Slavic *groza (“terror”). See there for cognates.

Inherited from Old East Slavic оудъ (udŭ, “limb, piece”), also found as оудо (udo), plural оудеса (udesa); from Proto-Slavic *udъ. Compare Old Church Slavonic оудъ (udŭ, “limb”), Bulgarian уд (ud, “limb”), Serbo-Croatian у̑д (“limb”), у́до (“piece of meat”), Slovene úd (“limb”) (tonal orthography),

Inherited from Old East Slavic уда (uda), from Proto-Slavic *ǫda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *and-, *end-. Cognate with Ukrainian ву́дка (vúdka), Belarusian вуда́ (vudá), Church Slavonic ѫда (ǫda), ѫдица (ǫdica), Bulgarian въ́дица (vắdica), Serbo-Croatian у̏дица, Slovene ȯ́dica (tonal orthography), Cze

parole.significato: to strike, to knock, to hit, to punch
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *udariti. See also удар (udar), драть (dratʹ) and раздо́р (razdór).

parole.significato: good luck, success (achievement of one's aim or goal)
parole.testo: Derived from уда́ться (udátʹsja), and then у- (u-) + дать (datʹ). Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti (“to give”), whence English donate, date and data.

From Proto-Slavic *ǫdidlo, a derivative of *ǫda. Related to уда (fishing rod) in the sense of "that which is inserted". The horse's bridle and fishing tackle evolved from the same concept related to holding, capturing, and securing. In the case of a horse, it refers to the metal piece inserted into
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *udobьnъ.

parole.significato: to distress, to deject, to cause to be depressed, to sadden, to aggrieve
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *udrǫčiti, from *drǫčiti. Compare Old Church Slavonic оудрѫчити (udrǫčiti, “to distress”), Polish dręczyć (“to torment”). Ultimately related to Russian друк (druk, “lever, pole”), Old Church Slavonic дрѫгъ (drǫgŭ, “beam, log”), Bulgarian дръг (drăg, “pole”), archaic Serbo
Inherited from Old East Slavic ѫжь (ǫžĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫžь. Cognates include Latin anguis, Old Prussian angis, Lithuanian angis, Latvian odze, Old High German unc and Old Armenian աւձ (awj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic ужасъ (užasŭ), from Proto-Slavic *užasъ (“amazement, horror”).

parole.significato: to terrify, to horrify, to awe, to appall
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žasnǫti.

parole.significato: already; carries the sense of the perfect continuous tenses in English.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *(j)uže.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ужина (užina, “afternoon snack; evening meal”), from Proto-Slavic *južina (“meal at noon”), from *jugъ (“South, south wind”). Compare Old East Slavic угъ (ugŭ, “South, noon”). The meaning evolved like this: "south" ⇒ "the time of the day when the sun is in the south" ⇒
Inherited from Old East Slavic узда (uzda), from Proto-Slavic *uzda. Compare Bulgarian юзда́ (juzdá), Czech uzda, Macedonian узда (uzda), Polish uzda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫzlъ (“knot”). Doublet of ве́нзель (vénzelʹ), a borrowing from Polish węzeł. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic ѫзлъ (ǫzlŭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫza, the form derives from the plural (*ǫzy).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ujь. Cognates include Polish wuj, Slovak ujo, Slovene ujec, Serbo-Croatian ујак, ujak, also ујко, ujko, Bulgarian вуйчо (vujčo), Macedonian вујко (vujko). Non-Slavic cognates include Old Prussian avis (“maternal uncle”), Gothic 𐌰𐍅𐍉 (awō, “grandmother”), Latin avus, Old A

parole.significato: lots, heaps, a tremendous lot, masses
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ujьma, related to *ęti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uklěja.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ukrasti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ukropъ. Sense 7 mocks the similarity of the word with the name Украи́на (Ukraína), and the use of the dill plant (Anethum graveolens) in traditional Ukrainian cuisine.
From Proto-Slavic *ulьjь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic улица (ulica), from Proto-Slavic *ulica.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ulovъka. Equivalent to улови́ть (ulovítʹ) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ulybъka. By surface analysis, улыба́ть(ся) (ulybátʹ(sja)) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Old East Slavic умъ (umŭ), from Proto-Slavic *umъ.
From Proto-Slavic *umerti, (*u- + *merti) from Proto-Indo-European *mer-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic оумѣти (uměti), from Proto-Slavic *uměti. Cognate to ум (um).

parole.significato: to lose heart, to be cast down, to be dejected or depressed
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic оуныти (unyti), from Proto-Slavic *nyti (“to yearn”). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + ныть (nytʹ, “to whimper, to whine, to ache”).

parole.significato: check (on someone), control, justice (a way to control someone's wilful or lawless acts)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *uprava.
у- + Proto-Slavic *prǫgъ
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь. Doublet of вампи́р (vampír).

Inherited from Old East Slavic уродъ (urodŭ, “feebleminded, witless, foolish”), from Proto-Slavic *ǫrodъ, ancient deverbative of *roditi with nominal negative prefix *ǫ-, zero grade of *ne, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uroďajь, whose middle part (*rodъ) yielded род (rod). Cognates include Polish urodzaj, Ukrainian врожа́й (vrožáj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic урокъ (urokŭ, “agreement, condition”), from Proto-Slavic *urokъ, Proto-Slavic root *rok-.

parole.significato: common practices, custom way of something
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *urędъ. Compare with Czech úřad, Slovak úrad, Polish urząd, Serbo-Croatian úred.

Inherited from Old East Slavic усъ (usŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫsъ < *vǫsъ < *vǫdsъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wónsa, from Proto-Indo-European *wondʰsom, s-expansion of root *wendʰ- (“hair, wool, beard”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫsatъ. By surface analysis, ус (us) + -а́тый (-átyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uslovьje. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + сло́во (slóvo) + -ие (-ije).

parole.significato: to fall asleep, to go to sleep
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *usъnǫti (“to fall asleep”), from *u- (“away”) + *sъpati (“to sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swep-.

parole.significato: to have time, to find time
parole.testo: By surface analysis, у- (u-) + спеть (spetʹ), from Proto-Slavic *spěti, from Proto-Indo-European *spewd- (“press, hurry”), whence English speed.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uspěxъ. Compare Ukrainian успіх (uspix).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *usta, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃éh₁os (“mouth”). Cognates include Sanskrit आस् (ās, “mouth”) and Latin ōs (“mouth”). Compare Polish usta.
From Proto-Slavic *ustьnъ. By surface analysis, уста́ (ustá) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic усторобити ся (ustorobiti sja), from Proto-Slavic *storbiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ustьje, from *usta + *-ьje. By surface analysis, уста́ (ustá) + -ье (-ʹje). Compare typologically Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma).
From у- (u-) + -сыпи́ть (-sypítʹ), causative of спать (spatʹ), from Old East Slavic съпати (sŭpati), from Proto-Slavic *sъpati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *utěxa.
By surface analysis, у́т(ка) (út(ka)) + -и́ный (-ínyj); compare Old East Slavic уты (uty), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtinъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙋтъка (utŭka), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtъka, diminutive of *ǫty. By surface analysis, уть (utʹ) + -ка (-ka). Cognate to Lithuanian antis, Germanic ant, and, Latin anas.
From Old East Slavic утьлъ (utĭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtьlъ
Inherited from Old East Slavic утъкъ (utŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtъkъ, from *ǫ- (Russian у- (u-)) + *tъkъ, cognate with or deverbal from *tъkati (Russian ткать (tkatʹ)).

parole.significato: to quench, to slake (thirst); to satisfy, to appease (hunger); to lull, to soothe, to alleviate (pain)
parole.testo: From у- (u-) + -толи́ть (-tolítʹ), from Proto-Slavic *toliti (“to calm, to soothe”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *utrьnъ. By surface analysis, у́тро (útro, “morning”) + -енный (-ennyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *(j)utro (“morning, dawn”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic утроба (utroba), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtroba (“internal organs”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic уха (uxa), from Proto-Slavic *juxa, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yew(ǝ)- (“to blend, mix (food), knead”). Cognates include Latin ius (whence English juice), Ancient Greek ζύμη (zúmē) (whence Russian энзи́м (enzím, “enzyme, ferment”)), Proto-Germanic *justaz, Sa

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uxo, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws. Cognate with Old Armenian ունկն (unkn), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐍃𐍉 (ausō), Ancient Greek οὖς (oûs), Latin auris, Persian هوش (huš, hôš, “intellect”).
From Proto-Slavic *učęstьnikъ. By surface analysis, уча́стие (učástije) + -ник (-nik).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *učęstь. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + часть (častʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *učenikъ.
From Proto-Slavic *učiteľь.

parole.significato: to teach, to instruct (often not in an academic setting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic учити (učiti), from Proto-Slavic *učiti.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *učьstivъ. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + чтить (čtitʹ, “to honour/honor, respect”) + -и́вый (-ívyj). Cognate with Polish uczciwy (“honest”), Czech uctivý (“respectful”), Serbo-Croatian у̀чтив (“polite”), Old Church Slavonic оучьтивъ (učĭtivŭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ušьnъ. By surface analysis, у́хо (úxo) + -но́й (-nój).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uščьrbъ. Compare Polish uszczerbek, Bulgarian щъ̀рбел (štằrbel) and Czech štěrba.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ujǫtъ, from *jǫtъ (“roof”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xalupa. Further etymology unknown. Compare Ukrainian халу́па (xalúpa), Belarusian халу́па (xalúpa), Polish chałupa, Czech chalupa, Slovak chalupa, Upper Sorbian chałupa, Lower Sorbian chałupa. The connection to Ancient Greek κᾰλῠ́βη (kălŭ́bē) and Ottoman Turkish قولبه (k
For "top of the boot" meaning: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoľeva. Cognate with Ukrainian халя́ва (xaljáva), Polish cholewa. Note also Ossetian хӕлаф (xælaf, “trousers”).

parole.significato: to grab (quickly); to steal; to take (from someone unlawfully)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xāpàti.

parole.significato: to expectorate (phlegm or spit), to spit (noisily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xъrkati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic хвала (xvala), from Proto-Slavic *xvala.
Inherited from Old East Slavic хвалити (xvaliti), from Proto-Slavic *xvaliti. By surface analysis, хвала́ (xvalá, “praise”) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).

parole.significato: to grasp, to grab, to seize, to snap, to snatch, to catch, to catch hold of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic хватати (xvatati), from Proto-Slavic *xvatati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvojьnъ. By surface analysis, хво́я (xvója) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvoroba or хворь (xvorʹ) + -оба (-oba).
Inherited from Old East Slavic хворостъ (xvorostŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xvorstъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvorъ, *xorъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvostъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Slavic *xvoščь, from *xvostъ (“tail”) + *-jь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvoja.

parole.significato: hovel, shack (a small, crudely built house)
parole.testo: Cognate with dialectal хиба́ть (xibátʹ, “to sway”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xybъ (“wobble”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xyžina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xylъ. Related to Bulgarian хилав (hilav, “feeble”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xyrěti.

parole.significato: sly person; crafty fellow, dodger, slyboots
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xytrьcь. By surface analysis, хи́трый (xítryj) + -ец (-ec). Cognate with Polish chytrzec.

parole.significato: to be sly/cunning/crafty, to try to fool
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xytriti. By surface analysis, хи́трый (xítryj) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
From Old East Slavic хытрость (xytrostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *xytrostь, from *xytrъ + *-ostь. By surface analysis, хи́трый (xítryj) + -ость (-ostʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic хытръ (xytrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlamъ/*xlomъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic хлѣбъ (xlěbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xlěbъ, from Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃 (hlaifs), from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz, of unknown origin. Cognate with English loaf, lady, lord.

parole.significato: to eat (liquid food with a spoon), to slurp
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlebati.

parole.significato: bread box, bread bin (a container for storing bread)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlěbьnica.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlěbьnъ. By surface analysis, хлеб (xleb) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlěvъ (“stall”).

parole.significato: to lash, to switch, to whip
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlestati. See also хлыст (xlyst, “whip”).

Dialectally also хли́бкий (xlíbkij), хлибко́й (xlibkój), хли́бый (xlíbyj); inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlibъkъ. Cognate with хли́бать (xlíbatʹ, “to fall ill, to shake from weakness”), also хли́бить (xlíbitʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlopati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klopotъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlynǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xlębь. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic хлѧбь (xlębĭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xъmelь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xmuriti.

parole.significato: gloomy, sullen (affected with, or expressing, gloom; melancholy)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xmura (“a cloud”), related to *xmuriti (“to make cloudy”). Cognates include Polish pochmurny (“cloudy”), Ukrainian похму́рий (poxmúryj, “cloudy, gloomy”). Possibly related to па́смурный (pásmurnyj).

parole.significato: trunk (extended nasal organ of an elephant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xobotъ. Cognate with Belarusian хо́бат (xóbat).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xovati.

parole.significato: motion, movement, travel, progress, locomotion, headway
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ходъ (xodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xodъ, from Proto-Indo-European *sod-, whence Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “threshold; road, path, journey”) and thereby English suffix -ode.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoditi.

parole.significato: fast, quick, going or able to go at a good clip
parole.testo: From ходи́ть (xodítʹ) + -кий (-kij), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xodъ. Compare Polish chodliwy for both etymological and semantic development.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoduľa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xodьba, from *xoditi + *-ьba. By surface analysis, ходи́ть (xodítʹ) + -ьба (-ʹba).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xodę̀ťь. Equivalent to ходи́ть (xodítʹ) + -я́чий (-jáčij). Doublet of ходя́щий (xodjáščij), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoliti. By surface analysis, хо́ля (xólja) + -ить (-itʹ).

parole.significato: withers (part of the back of a draft animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xolъka. Per Vasmer, probably derived from хохо́л (xoxól, “crest”) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xъlmъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoldъ (“coolness, cold”). Doublet of хлад (xlad), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xolditi. By surface analysis, хо́лод (xólod) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoldьnъ. Doublet of хла́дный (xládnyj), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. By surface analysis, хо́лод (xólod) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xolpъ. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic хлапъ (xlapŭ) with the same meaning or Polish chłop (“peasant”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xolstъ. Compare Old Church Slavonic хластъ (xlastŭ), Slovene hlȃst, Ukrainian хо́лост (xólost).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xolujь.
Inherited from Old East Slavic хомоуть (xomutĭ), from Proto-Slavic *xomǫtъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic хомѧкъ (xomękŭ), хомѣкъ (xoměkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xomě̀kъ, from *xoměstorъ (“hamster”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xъrvatъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic хоробръ (xorobrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xorbrъ. Cognate with Belarusian харо́бры (xaróbry). Doublet of хра́брый (xrábryj, “brave”), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: a large wooden house in traditional Russian architecture, especially if composed of separate heated sections connected…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic хоромъ (xoromŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xormъ. Doublet of храм (xram), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xorniti; compare its borrowed doublet храни́ть (xranítʹ). Compare typologically Proto-Germanic *burgijaną (whence English bury) (<< Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ-, whence also бере́чь (beréčʹ), English borrow)

Inherited from Old East Slavic хорошь (xorošĭ) (13th century), from Proto-Slavic *xoroščьnъ, from *xorostь (“beauty, pleasantness; convenience”) + *-ьnъ. Cognate with Ukrainian хоро́ший (xoróšyj), Belarusian харо́шы (xaróšy).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xorǫgy.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъxorь (literally “ferret, stinky”). Cognate to дух (dux), дохну́ть (doxnútʹ).
Diminutive of хорь (xorʹ), inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъxorь (literally “ferret, stinky”)
Inherited from Old East Slavic хотѣти (xotěti), from Proto-Slavic *xotěti.

parole.significato: (birds) crest, (human hair) topknot, tuft of hair
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic *хохолъ (*xoxolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xoxolъ < *koxolъ. Compare Polish chochoł, Polish chachoł and Czech chochol. The usage in reference to Ukrainian people comes from the оселе́дець (oselédecʹ), a traditional top-knot used by Ukrainian men. It acquired a derogatory co
According to Vasmer, from Proto-Slavic *xoxotъ, related to *xoxotati (“to laugh loudly”).

parole.significato: to laugh loudly, to laugh heartily, to roar with laughter, to guffaw
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoxotati.

parole.significato: to snore (breathe during sleep with harsh noises)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xrapěti.

Inherited from Old East Slavic шишька (šišĭka), from Proto-Slavic *šišьka.

parole.significato: to loaf about, to gad about
parole.testo: Dialectally also сля́ться (sljátʹsja). Per Vasmer, quoting Sobolevsky, probably from Proto-Slavic *sъljati sę, from *sъlati (“to send”) (whence Russian слать (slatʹ)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьmeľь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šьvъ. Compare шить (šitʹ). See Proto-Slavic *šiti for more information.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šumъ.

parole.significato: to make a noise; to be noisy; to rustle (e.g. of leaves)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šuměti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šumьnъ. By surface analysis, шум (šum) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šurь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šustrъ.

parole.significato: fool, jester (person in a mediaeval royal court)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic шутъ (šutŭ), from Proto-Slavic *šutъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šutiti.

parole.significato: whisper (the act of speaking in a quiet voice)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьčavь, *sьčavьľь. Sense 2 was coined on TikTok since 2024.
Inherited from Old East Slavic щадѣти (ščaděti, “to keep, spare”), from Proto-Slavic *ščęditi, from Proto-Indo-European *skend-. See also ску́дный (skúdnyj).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščebьňь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”). Related to ско́бель (skóbelʹ, “shaving/drawing knife, spokeshave”), скобли́ть (skoblítʹ, “to scrape, to scrub”), щебло́ (ščebló, “splinter, chip”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьbьtъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьbьtati. By surface analysis, ще́бет (ščébet) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščegъlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščeka. Cognate with Belarusian шчака́ (ščaká) and Ukrainian щока́ (ščoká).

parole.significato: to tickle, to titillate (touch repeatedly or stroke delicately)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьkъtati. Compare Old Church Slavonic скъкътати (skŭkŭtati) or скоктати (skoktati) (Russian recension), Serbo-Croatian škakljati, Slovene ščegetati, Macedonian скокотка (skokotka).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščelь. Cognates include Ukrainian щіль (ščilʹ), щі́лина (ščílyna), щіли́на (ščilýna), Belarusian шчэ́ль (ščélʹ), шчэ́лка (ščélka), шчы́ліна (ščýlina), Polish szczelina, Slovene ščálja.

parole.significato: to pinch (to cause pain or discomfort by pressing strongly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sčemiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic щенѧ (ščenę) + -ок (-ok), from Proto-Slavic *ščenę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščepa, from *skopiti (“to castrate”), from Proto-Indo-European *skēp-. Cognate with German Schüppe.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščepati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьrba + -ина (-ina).

parole.significato: bristles (of animal hair or a brush)

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščirъ.

parole.significato: pike (any freshwater fish of the genus Esox, a relatively large, predatory fish)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščùka.

Cognate with Ukrainian щу́плий (ščúplyj, “skinny, unattractive”), also щупля́вий (ščupljávyj); Belarusian шчу́плы (ščúply, “skinny, unattractive”); Czech štíplý (“lean, slender”); Slovak šťúply (“slender, thi

parole.significato: synonym of я́блоневый (jáblonevyj, “pertaining to apple trees”)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic ꙗблоньнꙑи (jablonĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *ablonьnъ. By surface analysis, я́блоня (jáblonja) + -ный (-nyj).

From Proto-Slavic *ablъčьnъ. By surface analysis, я́блоко (jábloko) + -ный (-nyj)

parole.significato: to show (to have someone see something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗвити (javiti), from Proto-Slavic *aviti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew- (“to perceive, see, be aware of”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *awiz (“obvious”) and Sanskrit आविस् (āvís, “manifestly, evidently”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *avьnъ. By surface analysis, явь (javʹ) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: lamb (flesh of a lamb used as food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agnętina. By surface analysis, ягня́та (jagnjáta, “lambs”) + -ина (-ina, suffix denoting a type of meat).
Inherited from Old East Slavic агнѧ (agnę), ꙗгнѧ (jagnę) + -ёнок (-jónok), from Proto-Slavic *agnę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷn-, the stem of *h₂egʷnós. Compare а́гнец (ágnec).
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗгода (jagoda), from Proto-Slavic *agoda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ṓˀgāˀ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agodica. By surface analysis, я́года (jágoda, “berry”) + -ица (-ica), because of the round shape of buttocks: compare the dialectal senses. Compare typologically ты́ква (týkva), ты́ковка (týkovka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agodьnъ. By surface analysis, я́года (jágoda) + -ный (-nyj)
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗдъ (jadŭ) / ѣдъ (jědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ědъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗловыи (jalovyi), from Proto-Slavic *jalovъ (“barren, infertile”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jariti. By surface analysis, я́рый (járyj) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗрьмъ (jarĭmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *arьmo, *arьmъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jarovъ, from *jaro (“spring”). Constructed as if from *яр (*jar) + -ово́й (-ovój); compare dialectal яр (jar, “heat, fire”), Old East Slavic ꙗра (jara, “spring”). First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: barley (annual temperate grasses of the species Hordeum vulgare or its grain used in making food and beverages)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗчьмꙑ (jačĭmy), from Proto-Slavic *ęčьmy. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἀκοστή (akostḗ, “barley”), Latin acus (“needle”) and Old English ahar (“corn-ear”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *aščerъka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ežь.

Most likely related to Proto-Slavic *oriti (“to drag down?”), whence разори́ть (razorítʹ). Not related to Latvian er̃rīgs (“angry, gloomy”), Latin errō (“to wander, get lost, err”), Old High German irri (“confused”) or Russian ёрш (jorš).

parole.significato: to fidget, to squirm, to move restlessly (to twist in discomfort, especially from shame or embarrassment)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьrzati, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erǵʰ- (“mount (sexually), cover, copulate”). Cognate to Lithuanian er̃žilas, ar̃žilas (“stallion”), aržùs (“hot-tempered, lustful”), Old Norse argr (“effeminate”), German arg (“bad”), English eerie.
